posts.title: Mixture of Experts: 671B Weights, 37B of Work
posts.subtitle: Sparse routing decouples how big a model is from how much it costs to run.
posts.summary: A Mixture-of-Experts layer replaces one big feed-forward block with many small ones and a router that picks a handful per token. That breaks the usual link between parameter count and FLOPs: DeepSeek-V3 holds 671B parameters but does the arithmetic of a 37B model. The cost you don't escape is memory — you still have to hold every expert.

slides.title: Every Token Pays for Every Parameter — Unless It Doesn't
slides.body: In a dense transformer, a 70B model multiplies all 70B weights for every single token. Mixture of Experts breaks that rule: the weights sit in memory, but each token only touches a slice of them.

slides.title: Dense Scaling Ties Capacity to Cost 1:1
slides.body: Scaling laws say more parameters means a better model. But in a dense network, doubling parameters doubles the FLOPs per token — and therefore latency and serving cost.
bullets: Roughly two-thirds of a transformer's parameters live in the feed-forward blocks, not attention.
Those blocks are where 'knowledge' concentrates — and where most of the per-token FLOPs go.
The uncomfortable question: does a token about Python syntax really need the weights that encode French poetry?

slides.title: Replace One FFN With N of Them, Plus a Router
slides.body: An MoE layer swaps the single feed-forward block for N smaller 'experts'. A tiny linear router scores all N for the incoming token, softmaxes the scores, and sends the token to only the top-k.
bullets: Router is one matrix: hidden_dim x N. Cost is negligible next to the experts themselves.
Output = weighted sum of the k chosen experts, using their router probabilities as weights.
Attention is untouched and stays dense — every token still attends over the full sequence.
Routing is per-token AND per-layer: the same token can hit completely different experts at layer 5 and layer 30.

slides.title: Fine-Grained Experts and the Shared Expert
slides.body: Modern MoE designs shrink each expert and raise k, so the router composes many small specialists instead of picking one of a few generalists. Some architectures also add an expert every token always uses.
bullets: Switch Transformer (2021) took the simplest route: top-1 routing, one expert per token, scaled to trillion-parameter models.
Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts per layer, router picks 2.
DeepSeek-V3: 256 routed experts per layer, router picks 8 — far finer slicing of the same capacity.
DeepSeek-V3 also keeps 1 shared expert that every token passes through, so common knowledge isn't duplicated 256 times.

slides.title: Total vs. Active Parameters, in Real Models
slides.body: The gap between the two columns is the whole point of MoE. DeepSeek-V3 activates about 5.5% of its parameters per token; Mixtral activates about 28%.
bullets: Switch Transformers reported up to 7x faster pre-training than dense T5 baselines at equal compute.
Mixtral matches or beats Llama 2 70B on benchmarks while doing the per-token arithmetic of a 12.9B model.

slides.title: Worked Example: Sizing a Box for Mixtral 8x7B
slides.body: Say you want to serve Mixtral 8x7B in bf16. Budget the memory from total parameters and the throughput from active parameters — they give completely different answers.
bullets: Memory: 46.7B params x 2 bytes = ~93 GB of weights. One 80 GB H100 is not enough; you need two, before any KV cache.
Compute: only 12.9B params multiply per token, so latency lands near a ~13B dense model, not a ~47B one.
Net effect: you buy 70B-class quality at 13B-class speed — and pay for it in VRAM, not in time.
DeepSeek-V3 makes the same trade far more extreme: ~670 GB of FP8 weights for 37B worth of arithmetic.

slides.title: Where MoE Hurts: Collapse, All-to-All, and Small Batches
slides.body: Sparsity is not free. Three failure modes bite in practice, and one of them can silently ruin a training run.
bullets: Routing collapse: nothing stops the router from funneling most tokens into a few experts. The rest never train, and your 671B model behaves like a small dense one.
The classic fix is an auxiliary load-balancing loss — but it fights the language-modeling objective. DeepSeek-V3 instead nudges a per-expert bias used only for routing, keeping the loss clean.
Expert parallelism means an all-to-all shuffle at every MoE layer. DeepSeek-V3 caps each token's routing to 4 nodes purely to bound that traffic.
Small batches waste it: with few tokens in flight, each expert gets a handful of rows and the GPU idles on weights you paid to load.

slides.title: When to Reach for MoE — and When Not To
bullets: MoE decouples capacity from compute: parameters set memory, active parameters set latency.
Best fit: high-throughput serving where big batches keep every expert busy and VRAM is available.
Worst fit: single-user local inference on one consumer GPU — you pay full memory for a fraction of the compute.
Always check the active-parameter count, not the headline one, when comparing an MoE model to a dense one.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total parameters and activates 37B per token. What does that imply for deployment?
options: You only need enough VRAM for 37B parameters
You need VRAM for all 671B, but the per-token compute is closer to a 37B model
Both memory and compute scale with 37B
Both memory and compute scale with 671B
questions.explanation: The router can pick any expert for any token, so all 671B parameters must be resident in memory. Only the 8 selected experts do arithmetic, so FLOPs per token track the 37B figure. Memory follows total params; latency follows active params.

questions.prompt: What is 'routing collapse' in an MoE model?
options: The router network runs out of memory during training
Experts are dropped when a node fails mid-training
The router sends most tokens to a small subset of experts, leaving the rest undertrained
Two experts learn identical weights and are merged
questions.explanation: Routing is a positive feedback loop: an expert that gets more tokens trains faster, so the router prefers it even more. Left unchecked, your huge sparse model effectively shrinks to a few active experts. Balancing schemes — an auxiliary loss, or DeepSeek-V3's routing-only bias term — exist to break that loop.

questions.prompt: Which workload is the WORST fit for a Mixture-of-Experts model?
options: A batched serving endpoint handling thousands of concurrent requests
Large-scale pre-training on a multi-node GPU cluster
Single-user chat on one consumer GPU with limited VRAM
A high-throughput document summarization pipeline
questions.explanation: MoE's win comes from spending memory to save compute, and it needs many tokens in flight so every expert gets a full batch. A single user on a memory-constrained GPU hits the worst of both: they must hold every expert, but never generate enough concurrent tokens to keep them busy.

posts.title: LLM-as-a-Judge: Grading What You Can't Unit Test
posts.subtitle: A model can score another model's output — but only if you know which way it cheats.
posts.summary: LLM-as-a-judge uses a strong model to score open-ended output that has no single correct answer. The MT-Bench study found GPT-4 agreed with human preferences about 85% of the time — above the 81% humans agreed with each other. It also documented the ways judges systematically cheat: position, verbosity, and self-preference.

slides.title: Your Best Feature Has No Assert Statement
slides.body: You can unit-test a JSON parser. You cannot unit-test 'was this summary faithful?' or 'was this support reply helpful?'. LLM-as-a-judge is the standard answer — and it comes with known, measurable biases.

slides.title: String Matching Died the Moment Output Got Open-Ended
slides.body: Classic NLP metrics score surface overlap with a reference answer. That breaks completely when many different answers are equally good.
bullets: BLEU/ROUGE punish a correct paraphrase and reward a fluent but wrong answer that reuses the reference's words.
Human evaluation is the real gold standard, but it costs hours per hundred examples — you can't run it on every pull request.
The gap this leaves: no fast, cheap signal for the exact qualities you actually shipped the feature for.

slides.title: Three Ways to Ask, With Very Different Properties
slides.body: 'LLM-as-a-judge' is not one technique. The framing you choose determines both the reliability and the failure mode you inherit.
bullets: Pointwise: 'score this answer 1-5.' Cheap and scales to one output at a time, but the scale drifts between runs.
Pairwise: 'is A or B better?' Far more stable, because relative judgments are easier than absolute ones.
Reference-guided: 'grade this against the gold answer.' The MT-Bench authors found this materially improves judging on math and reasoning, where an unaided judge reasons badly itself.

rows: Absolute scale drifts run to run
Which is better, A or B?
Position bias toward whichever came first
Only as good as the reference you wrote

slides.title: The Three Documented Ways Judges Cheat
slides.body: The MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena paper named these explicitly. Treat them as defaults you must design around, not edge cases.
bullets: Position bias: the same two answers, swapped, can flip the verdict. Fix by running both orders and only counting a win when it survives the swap.
Verbosity bias: longer answers win more, even when they add nothing. Fix by controlling for length or penalizing padding in the rubric.
Self-enhancement bias: a judge tends to favor output from itself or its own model family. Fix by never judging a model with itself.
Limited reasoning: a judge that can't solve the math problem can't reliably grade it either — hand it the reference solution.

slides.title: How Good Is a Judge, Actually?
slides.body: The headline result from the MT-Bench study: strong LLM judges land inside the noise band of human labelers themselves — which is the only bar that matters, since humans disagree with each other constantly.
bullets: GPT-4 judge vs. human preference: roughly 85% agreement.
Human vs. human on the same comparisons: about 81% agreement.
Read it correctly: the judge isn't 'right', it's about as consistent with a human as another human would be.
That also caps your ambition — a judge cannot be more reliable than the ceiling humans set.

slides.title: Worked Example: Grading RAG Faithfulness
slides.body: You ship a support bot over your docs. The failure you care about is a confident answer that the retrieved chunks never supported. Here's a judge that catches it.
bullets: Don't ask 'is this good, 1-10?'. Ask the judge to extract each factual claim in the answer, then mark each one supported / unsupported by the provided chunks.
Score = supported claims / total claims. Now it's a countable number, not a vibe.
Decompose first, score second: claim-level checks are far more stable than one holistic rating.
Calibrate before trusting: hand-label ~100 examples, measure how often the judge agrees, and only then wire it into CI.
Pin the judge's model version. A silent provider upgrade will move your metric and look like a regression in your app.

slides.title: When NOT to Use an LLM Judge
slides.body: A judge is a fast, biased approximation of a human. There are places where that trade is simply the wrong one.
bullets: Safety, legal, or compliance sign-off: shared blind spots mean the judge misses exactly what the generator got wrong.
Same-family judging: grading GPT output with GPT invites self-enhancement bias straight into your metric.
Fine-grained numeric claims ('quality rose from 7.1 to 7.3'): the judge's resolution isn't that good. Use pairwise win rates instead.
Anything with a real ground truth — exact-match, schema validation, or a passing test suite beats a judge every time, and costs less.

slides.title: The Short Version
bullets: Prefer pairwise comparisons over absolute 1-5 scores; they're measurably more stable.
Always swap positions and require the verdict to survive the swap.
Decompose into checkable claims instead of asking for one holistic number.
Calibrate against human labels once, pin the judge version, and re-check when either side changes.

questions.prompt: You ask a judge model 'which answer is better, A or B?' and it picks A. What is the cheapest way to check the verdict isn't position bias?
options: Re-run the same prompt with a higher temperature
Swap A and B and re-run; only count a win if the same answer wins both times
Ask the judge to explain its reasoning
Use a larger judge model
questions.explanation: Position bias means the ordering itself moves the verdict, so re-running in the same order — even with reasoning or a bigger model — reproduces the bias. Swapping and requiring consistency turns the bias into a detectable disagreement, which you can then score as a tie.

questions.prompt: On MT-Bench, a GPT-4 judge agreed with human preferences about 85% of the time, while humans agreed with each other about 81%. What's the right conclusion?
options: The judge is more correct than humans are
The judge is roughly as consistent with a human as another human is
The remaining 15% are judge hallucinations
Human evaluation should be abandoned
questions.explanation: There is no oracle here — 'correct' is defined by human preference, which is itself noisy at about 81% self-agreement. The judge sitting near that band means it's a usable stand-in, not that it's right. It also means human agreement is the ceiling, so chasing 95% judge accuracy is chasing noise.

questions.prompt: Which task should NOT be handed to an LLM judge?
options: Rating whether a support reply was helpful
Checking whether a summary's claims are supported by the source
Verifying that generated code passes the project's test suite
Comparing two prompt variants by win rate
questions.explanation: Running the test suite is real ground truth: it's deterministic, cheaper than an LLM call, and cannot be talked into a wrong answer. Reach for a judge only when no executable check exists — the other three options are all genuinely open-ended.

references.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv:2306.05685)

posts.title: DFlash: Drafting a Whole Block Before Verifying It
posts.subtitle: A diffusion drafter replaces the autoregressive bottleneck in speculative decoding.
posts.summary: DFlash replaces the small autoregressive draft model in speculative decoding with a lightweight block diffusion model that drafts an entire block in one forward pass. Independent benchmarks show it beating EAGLE-3 by roughly 2x-2.5x, and it's already shipped in vLLM's speculators library.

slides.title: Speculative Decoding's Draft Step Was Still the Bottleneck
slides.body: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by having a small model draft several tokens, then having the big model verify them in one pass. DFlash asks: why is the draft model still autoregressive?

slides.title: The Draft Model Drafts One Token at a Time
slides.body: Classic speculative decoding (and drafters like EAGLE-3) still generate their draft tokens sequentially, token by token. That serial chain caps how much latency you can hide, even though the draft model is small.
bullets: Each draft token still waits on the previous one — the draft phase is fast per-token, but not parallel.
Bigger draft trees (more candidate continuations) help acceptance rate but add more sequential steps, not fewer.
The target model's single verification pass is cheap; the serial drafting is what limits the ceiling.

slides.title: A Block Diffusion Model Drafts the Whole Block at Once
slides.body: DFlash swaps the autoregressive drafter for a lightweight block diffusion model, conditioned on hidden-state features pulled from the target model, that denoises an entire block of draft tokens in a single forward pass.
bullets: One forward pass produces a full candidate block instead of one token per step.
Conditioning on the target model's own context features keeps the draft distribution close to what the target would actually produce, which keeps acceptance rates high.
Verification stays exactly as in standard speculative decoding — output is provably identical to greedy/sampled decoding from the target model (lossless).

slides.title: Reported Speedups vs. EAGLE-3
slides.body: Independent write-ups (LMSYS Org, UC San Diego benchmarks) report DFlash consistently ahead of EAGLE-3 at matched tree size, with the gap widening under greedy decoding.
bullets: Headline claim: over 6x lossless acceleration overall, up to ~2.5x higher speedup than EAGLE-3.
UCSD single-stream benchmark on Qwen3-8B: DFlash ~4.86x avg vs EAGLE-3 ~1.76x avg at matched tree size.

slides.title: Production Impact: More Concurrent Users on the Same GPU
slides.body: This isn't just a benchmark number — it changes how many users one GPU can serve. On NVIDIA Blackwell hardware running TensorRT-LLM, DFlash was measured serving more than 15x the concurrent user load of standard autoregressive decoding at the same latency budget.
bullets: Throughput gains from faster drafting translate directly into serving cost per token.
DFlash checkpoints already exist for open models like Qwen3.8-27B and Muse-Glimmer-30B, so it's not just a research demo — it's integrated into vLLM's speculators library.

slides.title: When Block Diffusion Drafting Is Worth Adopting
slides.body: Use DFlash-style drafting when you're already running speculative decoding and drafting latency, not verification, is your bottleneck.
bullets: Best fit: high-throughput serving where GPU has slack to run a lightweight diffusion drafter alongside the target model.
Needs its own trained/fine-tuned drafter per target model family — it isn't a drop-in for every checkpoint on day one.
Block size is a tuning knob: larger blocks mean more parallelism but can lower acceptance rate on divergent continuations, so the sweet spot is workload-dependent.
Not a magic multiplier if you're already compute-bound with large batches — the free lunch comes from underused GPU cycles during the draft step.

questions.prompt: What was the actual bottleneck DFlash targets in standard speculative decoding?
options: The target model's verification pass is too slow
The draft model still generates its candidate tokens one at a time, sequentially
GPUs can't run two models simultaneously
KV cache memory runs out during drafting
questions.explanation: Verification by the target model is a single cheap forward pass. The draft phase was the serial bottleneck because even small autoregressive drafters still generate token-by-token.

questions.prompt: How does DFlash's block diffusion drafter stay lossless (produce output identical to the target model)?
options: It replaces the target model entirely
It shrinks the vocabulary to reduce ambiguity
Verification against the target model still happens exactly as in standard speculative decoding — only the drafting step changed
It rounds probabilities to remove low-likelihood tokens
questions.explanation: Losslessness in speculative decoding comes from the verification step, not the drafter. DFlash only changes how draft candidates are generated (in parallel via diffusion); the target model still verifies every token exactly.

questions.prompt: What's a real tradeoff of increasing DFlash's block size?
options: It has no effect on performance
Larger blocks always increase acceptance rate
Larger blocks add more parallelism but can lower acceptance rate on continuations that diverge more from the conditioned context
Larger blocks require a bigger target model
questions.explanation: Block size is a real tuning knob — bigger blocks parallelize more drafting work, but the diffusion model has to commit to more tokens at once, which can hurt acceptance when the true continuation branches unpredictably.

posts.title: OpenAI Gates Its Most Capable Model Behind a Trust List
posts.subtitle: Daybreak splits into a defender tier and a locked-down offensive-capability tier.
posts.summary: OpenAI expanded Daybreak, its cyber defense program, into two tiers: a broadly-available defensive model and a far more capable offensive-research model restricted to vetted partners. The gap between them — 1.5% vs 95% success on high-risk exploit tasks — is the real story.

slides.title: OpenAI Splits Daybreak Into a Defender Tier and a Locked Tier
slides.body: OpenAI expanded its Daybreak cyber-defense program with two models built for opposite audiences: one for defenders everywhere, one for a short list of vetted partners.

slides.title: The Defense Window Is Narrowing
slides.body: Attackers are already using AI to accelerate exploit development. Defenders need equally capable tools, but a model that's great at finding zero-days is, by construction, also great at exploit chain development — the same capability cuts both ways.
bullets: A model strong enough to find a real zero-day is strong enough to help build one.
Releasing that capability broadly helps attackers as much as defenders — so OpenAI split access instead of picking one tradeoff for everyone.

slides.title: Two Tiers, Two Different Models
slides.body: Daybreak Blue runs GPT-5.6 Sol with safety recalibrated for defensive work. Daybreak Red runs GPT-5.6 Cyber, trained specifically for offense-style tasks, and is only available to trusted partners.
bullets: Daybreak Blue (GPT-5.6 Sol): vulnerability discovery, detection engineering, incident response, patch validation — open to defenders broadly.
Daybreak Red (GPT-5.6 Cyber): zero-day discovery and exploit chain development — access gated to named trusted partners only.

slides.title: The Capability Gap Is the Whole Point
slides.body: OpenAI's own security evaluation tested both models on high-risk tasks: exploit chain development, authentication bypass, privilege escalation.
bullets: That ~60x gap is what justifies gating Cyber to a short partner list instead of general release.

headers: Success rate on high-risk exploit tasks

slides.title: Rollout: Vendor Partnerships and Cloud Access
slides.body: The expansion shipped alongside partnerships with roughly 16 cybersecurity vendors, and OpenAI's cyber models became available to eligible customers on Amazon Bedrock.
bullets: Reported partners include names like Accenture, IBM, CrowdStrike, and Cloudflare.
Amazon Bedrock listed the models for eligible customers on August 11, 2026 — distribution through existing enterprise cloud channels, not a public API.

slides.title: Access Control Is Now Part of the Model Release Itself
slides.body: This is less a capability story than an access-control story: the model card decides who gets it, not just what it can do.
bullets: "Trusted partner" gating is doing real safety work here — it's not marketing, given the 60x capability gap on offensive tasks.
It also concentrates powerful offensive-security AI in a small set of vetted organizations, which raises its own governance questions about who decides "trusted."
Smaller defenders without a partner relationship still only get the weaker Blue tier.

questions.prompt: Why did OpenAI split Daybreak into two separate models instead of releasing one?
options: To charge two different prices
Because a model capable enough to find real zero-days is also capable enough to help build exploits, so broad release of the stronger model would help attackers too
GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Cyber are unrelated products
To comply with a specific government mandate named in the announcement
questions.explanation: The dual-use nature of offensive security capability is the core reason: the same skill that finds a zero-day for a defender can build an exploit for an attacker, so OpenAI gated the stronger model to vetted partners instead of general release.

questions.prompt: In OpenAI's security evaluation, roughly what was the gap between the two models on high-risk exploit tasks?
options: No meaningful difference
GPT-5.6 Sol succeeded ~1.5% of the time vs. ~95% for GPT-5.6 Cyber
Both succeeded above 90%
GPT-5.6 Cyber failed more often than Sol
questions.explanation: OpenAI reported Sol (the broadly-available defensive model) succeeding on about 1.5% of high-risk requests like exploit chain development, versus about 95% for Cyber (the gated model) — a roughly 60x gap that underpins the access restriction.

questions.prompt: How is Daybreak Red (GPT-5.6 Cyber) distributed?
options: Open weights on Hugging Face
Free public API access
Restricted to a short list of trusted partners, plus availability to eligible customers via Amazon Bedrock
Only available inside OpenAI's internal red team
questions.explanation: Access is gated to named trusted partners (reported to include firms like Accenture, IBM, CrowdStrike, and Cloudflare), with cloud distribution through Amazon Bedrock for eligible customers rather than open or public API access.

posts.title: Hybrid Search: Why RAG Still Needs Keywords
posts.subtitle: Dense embeddings miss exact strings — a sparse retriever catches what they smear away.
posts.summary: Dense vector search is great at paraphrase and semantic similarity but quietly fails on exact strings like error codes, SKUs, and rare proper nouns. Hybrid search runs a lexical retriever (BM25) alongside dense retrieval and fuses the two ranked lists, usually with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, to catch both.

slides.title: Your Embedding Model Doesn't Know What 'E0442' Means
slides.body: Dense retrieval is excellent at semantic similarity and terrible at exact strings. Hybrid search fixes that by never relying on embeddings alone.

slides.title: Embeddings Smear Rare Tokens Into a Similarity Space
slides.body: A dense retriever encodes text into a vector and ranks documents by cosine similarity. That works great for paraphrase, but rare tokens (codes, SKUs, acronyms, numbers) get compressed into the same neighborhood as semantically related — but textually wrong — content.
bullets: Query "error E0442" can retrieve semantically-similar troubleshooting docs while missing the one doc that literally contains "E0442."
The failure is silent: there's no error, no exception — just a wrong-but-plausible-looking top result.
This gets worse for domain-specific jargon the embedding model never saw much of during training.

slides.title: Run a Lexical Retriever Alongside the Dense One
slides.body: Hybrid search adds BM25 — a sparse, TF-IDF-style lexical scorer with no training required — as a second retrieval path that runs in parallel with dense vector search, then merges both ranked lists.
bullets: BM25 scores documents on exact term overlap and term rarity — it will always surface the doc containing "E0442" verbatim.
Dense retrieval still handles paraphrase and semantic queries the lexical side can't touch.
Both retrievers query the same document set independently; nothing is chosen upfront, both always run.

slides.title: Fusing Two Rankings Without Comparable Scores
slides.body: BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on different, incomparable scales — you can't just average them. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps that by using rank position instead of raw score.
bullets: RRF score for a document d: sum over each retriever of 1 / (k + rank_d), with k typically set to 60.
A document ranked #1 by BM25 and #3 by dense search scores higher than one ranked #50 by both — no score normalization needed.
Cheap to compute and doesn't require retraining anything when you swap the embedding model or the lexical index.

slides.title: What Each Retriever Is Actually Good At

rows: Exact terms, codes, rare words, zero training needed
Exact strings, sensitive to domain shift from training data
Two indexes to maintain, extra retrieval pass, fusion tuning

slides.title: One Search Box, Two Very Different Queries
slides.body: An internal support-ticket search has to handle both "how do I reset MFA" (paraphrase-heavy, no exact terms) and "TOTP-6821" (an exact ticket code) in the same search box.
bullets: Dense-only retrieval nails the first query and can completely miss the second — the code is just a token to the embedding model.
BM25-only nails the second query but returns nothing useful for the paraphrased first one if the ticket never uses the words "reset" or "MFA" verbatim.
Hybrid retrieval handles both classes of query in the same pipeline, because both retrievers always run.

slides.title: When Hybrid Search Is Worth the Extra Infrastructure
slides.body: Hybrid search is a real cost — two indexes, two retrieval passes, a fusion step to tune — not a free upgrade.
bullets: Worth it when your queries mix exact identifiers (codes, SKUs, error strings) with natural-language paraphrase — support search, code search, e-commerce, legal/medical retrieval.
Skip it if your corpus and queries are pure natural language with no exact-match requirement — dense-only is simpler and cheaper to run.
RRF's k parameter and any per-retriever weighting still need tuning against your real query distribution — hybrid isn't fire-and-forget.
Reranking (a cross-encoder pass on the fused top-K) is the natural next layer on top of hybrid retrieval, not a replacement for it.

questions.prompt: Why can pure dense (embedding) retrieval fail on a query like an exact error code?
options: Dense retrieval only works on English text
Embedding models compress rare/exact tokens into a similarity space where textual exactness gets lost, so a semantically-similar-but-wrong doc can outrank the exact match
Dense retrieval is always slower than BM25
Error codes are filtered out of vector indexes by default
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity over embeddings rewards semantic closeness, not exact string match — so a document that never contains the exact code can still rank above the one that does, silently.

questions.prompt: Why does Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) use rank position instead of raw retriever scores?
options: Rank is faster to compute than any score
BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on incomparable scales, so combining raw scores would require normalization; rank position sidesteps that entirely
RRF only works with two retrievers, never more
Raw scores are not available from BM25 implementations
questions.explanation: You can't directly average a BM25 score and a cosine similarity — they're not on the same scale. RRF avoids the normalization problem by scoring purely on each document's rank position in each list.

questions.prompt: When is hybrid search NOT worth the added infrastructure?
options: When your corpus has no exact-match identifiers and queries are pure natural-language paraphrase
Whenever you have more than 1000 documents
Whenever latency matters at all
Hybrid search is always worth it regardless of query patterns
questions.explanation: If nothing in your query distribution needs exact-string matching, a dense-only pipeline is simpler and cheaper — hybrid search earns its cost specifically when exact identifiers and paraphrase both show up in real queries.

posts.title: MCP Tools: The Primitive Everything Else Wraps
posts.subtitle: Discovery, invocation, and the annotations that tell an agent when to ask first.
posts.summary: MCP Tools give a server a standard way to expose executable actions to a model: a discoverable list, a structured call/response cycle, and annotations that describe risk before anything runs. They're the one primitive the model invokes on its own initiative — and the one most agent tool-use is quietly built on top of.

slides.title: The Model Context Protocol Has Four Primitives. Tools Do the Work.
bullets: Resources = data the app attaches
Prompts = templates the user invokes
Sampling = server asks the model
Tools = the model asks the server to act

slides.title: Function Calling Alone Doesn't Scale Across Servers
slides.body: Before MCP, every app that wanted an LLM to call functions defined its own schema, wiring, and trust model. A tool built for one agent didn't work in another. MCP standardizes the wire format so any MCP client can call any MCP server's tools without custom glue.
bullets: Every framework had its own function-schema dialect
No standard way to discover what a server could do at runtime
No shared vocabulary for 'this action is dangerous'

slides.title: tools/list Advertises, tools/call Executes
slides.body: A client sends tools/list and gets back each tool's name, description, and a JSON Schema for its input. To run one, the client sends tools/call with the tool name and arguments; the server returns content blocks (text, images, embedded resources) plus an isError flag.
bullets: Discovery and invocation are two separate JSON-RPC methods
Input is validated against the tool's own inputSchema before it runs
A tool can also declare an outputSchema for structured results
notifications/tools/list_changed tells the client the set just changed

slides.title: Annotations Are a Risk Vocabulary, Not a Sandbox
slides.body: Each tool can carry hints: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint. They tell a client what kind of confirmation UI to show — they are not enforced by the protocol, so a compromised server can lie about them.

rows: Tool only observes, never mutates state
Repeating the same call changes nothing further
Tool reaches outside a closed, known set of entities

slides.title: A File-Editing Server, Annotated Correctly
bullets: list_files -> readOnlyHint: true, so a trusted client auto-approves it
read_file -> readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false
write_file -> readOnlyHint: false, destructiveHint: true -> client shows a confirmation dialog before it runs
delete_file -> destructiveHint: true, idempotentHint: true -> deleting twice is safe, but the client still asks first

slides.title: Tools vs. the Other Three Primitives

rows: Static or slow-changing context (files, DB rows)

slides.title: Where Tool Annotations Break Down
slides.body: Annotations are hints the server chooses to set — nothing stops a compromised or careless server from marking a destructive action readOnlyHint: true. Treat them as UX signals for trusted servers, not a security boundary.
bullets: Never treat an unverified server's hints as ground truth
Large tool lists (50+) also blow up the context window and confuse routing — namespace or filter before exposing them all
A tool with no outputSchema returns unstructured content the model must parse itself

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Tools are MCP's only agent-initiated primitive — the other three flow app/user -> model
Discovery (tools/list) and execution (tools/call) are separate calls, so a client can inspect and filter before ever running one
Annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) are hints for UX, not a trust boundary
list_changed notifications let a server add or remove tools mid-session without a full reconnect

questions.prompt: In MCP, which primitive lets the model itself decide to take an action?
options: Resources
Prompts
Sampling
Tools
questions.explanation: Tools are the one primitive the model invokes on its own initiative during a task; Resources are attached by the app, Prompts are triggered by the user, and Sampling is the server asking the model for a completion.

questions.prompt: A tool has destructiveHint: true and readOnlyHint: false. What should a client typically do before calling it?
options: Auto-approve silently, since MCP verifies safety server-side
Refuse to call it under any circumstances
Show the user a confirmation step before invoking it
Ignore the annotation and call tools/list instead
questions.explanation: Annotations are UX hints. A destructive, non-read-only tool is exactly the case a well-behaved client should pause on and ask the user to confirm — MCP itself doesn't enforce this, the client does.

questions.prompt: Why does MCP separate tools/list from tools/call into two distinct methods?
options: Because JSON-RPC requires every action to have exactly two calls
So a client can discover and filter what's available before committing to run anything
Because tools/list is deprecated in favor of tools/call
To force the model to call every listed tool once per session
questions.explanation: Separating discovery from execution lets a client inspect a tool's schema and annotations, decide whether to expose it to the model at all, and validate arguments — all before any side effect happens.

posts.title: Agent Skills: Why They Work, Until They Don't
posts.subtitle: Procedural anchoring explains 65.7% of when skills help — and retrieval sinks the rest.
posts.summary: A new study feeds agents the exact same past trajectories in two packagings — raw Workflow Memory versus a distilled SKILL.md — and finds packaging matters more than content: the distilled version wins by about 6 points, mostly by stabilizing execution rather than teaching new facts. But retrieval precision collapses as the skill library grows, from 29.6% at 5 candidates to 3.3% at 100.

slides.title: Skills Aren't Knowledge — They're a Procedure the Agent Can Follow
bullets: Compares the same past agent trajectories packaged two ways: raw Workflow Memory vs. a distilled SKILL.md
The distilled version wins by about 6 percentage points on task success
The paper traces exactly why — and where the approach breaks down as the skill library grows

slides.title: More Agent Experience Doesn't Automatically Mean a Better Agent
slides.body: Agents that log their own past trajectories can, in principle, reuse that experience on later tasks. But raw trajectory logs are noisy: they mix useful steps with dead ends, retries, and irrelevant tool output. Feeding that back directly as 'memory' often helps less than expected.
bullets: Workflow Memory keeps most of the raw execution detail from past runs
Noise and process drift in that raw log can mislead the agent on a new, similar task
Open question: does packaging the same experience differently — as a distilled procedure — change outcomes, or is it the same information either way?

slides.title: Distill Trajectories Into a SKILL.md, Not a Log
slides.body: The paper compares agents given the identical underlying trajectories in two forms: full Workflow Memory versus a distilled SKILL.md — a compact procedural summary of setup, steps, what to check, and common mistakes to avoid.
bullets: Same source experience, two packagings: raw log vs. distilled procedure
SKILL.md format outperforms raw Workflow Memory by about 6.06 percentage points on task success
The mechanism they identify: 'procedural anchoring' — skills mainly stabilize what to do first, which tool to use, and what to verify, not inject facts the agent didn't already have

slides.title: Where the Benefit Actually Comes From

rows: Procedural anchoring — stabilizes what to do, which tool, what to verify
Explicit knowledge injection — supplies a missing fact

slides.title: Worked Example: Retrieval Precision Collapses as the Library Grows
slides.body: The same skill-based approach was tested with retrieval pools of different sizes — simulating a growing library of saved skills the agent has to search before picking one.
bullets: With a pool of 5 candidate skills, the skill actually used was the correct/relevant one 29.6% of the time
Grow the pool to 100 skills and that precision drops to 3.3%
The bottleneck isn't the skill format itself — it's retrieval: finding the right skill among many becomes the hard part long before the skills themselves stop being useful

slides.title: When a Skill Actively Hurts
slides.body: The paper's other headline finding is about failure modes: skills aren't universally safe to apply.
bullets: A skill written for one context, applied rigidly in an incompatible one, can actively steer the agent wrong
Brittle assumptions baked into a skill (a specific file layout, a specific tool version) break silently when the environment shifts
Because retrieval precision degrades with library size, blindly growing a skill library is not a free lunch — curation and better retrieval matter more than sheer skill count

slides.title: The Practical Takeaway for Skill Authors
bullets: Write skills as tight procedures (setup -> steps -> checks -> common mistakes), not knowledge dumps — that's the part shown to actually move the needle
Don't assume a bigger skill library is strictly better — retrieval precision is the real constraint, not skill quality alone
Scope each skill narrowly enough that its assumptions (environment, tool versions, file layout) stay valid wherever it gets retrieved

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: SKILL.md-style distilled procedures beat raw workflow-memory logs by about 6 points on the same underlying experience
65.7% of the benefit comes from procedural anchoring (stabilizing execution), only 4.5% from injecting new facts
Retrieval precision — not skill quality — is the scaling bottleneck: 29.6% at a 5-skill pool falls to 3.3% at 100
A skill applied outside the context it was written for can actively hurt; write narrow, well-scoped skills over broad ones

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what mechanism accounts for the largest share (65.7%) of cases where a skill helped an agent succeed?
options: Injecting a new fact the agent didn't know
Procedural anchoring — stabilizing what to do first, which tool, what to verify
Using a larger context window
Switching to a bigger base model
questions.explanation: The paper found skills work mainly by stabilizing execution order and tool choice, not by teaching the agent new facts — that knowledge-injection path accounted for only 4.5% of cases.

questions.prompt: What happens to retrieval precision as the skill library grows from 5 to 100 candidate skills?
options: It stays roughly constant since more skills means more coverage
It improves, since a bigger library is more likely to contain the right skill
It drops sharply, from 29.6% to 3.3%
It becomes irrelevant because agents ignore retrieval past 10 skills
questions.explanation: As the candidate pool grows, the agent's actually-used skill is far less likely to be the right one — precision falls from 29.6% at a pool of 5 to 3.3% at a pool of 100. Retrieval, not skill quality, becomes the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Why can a skill written for one context actively hurt when applied in another?
options: Skills are cryptographically signed to a single environment
Its baked-in assumptions (file layout, tool versions) can silently be wrong in the new context
MCP blocks skills from being reused across sessions
Skills expire automatically after one use
questions.explanation: A skill is a distilled procedure tied to the assumptions of the context it was written in. Applied rigidly somewhere those assumptions don't hold, it steers the agent through steps that no longer make sense — one of the paper's core failure modes.

posts.title: GPT-Live: OpenAI's Full-Duplex Voice Model
posts.subtitle: Listening and speaking at once, with a live handoff to GPT-5.5 for anything it can't do in-voice.
posts.summary: OpenAI replaced ChatGPT's turn-based Advanced Voice Mode with GPT-Live, a full-duplex voice model that listens and speaks simultaneously and can be interrupted mid-sentence. When a request needs real reasoning or tools, GPT-Live hands off to GPT-5.5 running in parallel rather than trying to do it in-voice.

slides.title: Voice AI Stops Waiting Its Turn
bullets: GPT-Live replaces Advanced Voice Mode as ChatGPT's default voice model
Full-duplex: it processes incoming speech and generates outgoing speech at the same time
Ships as two sizes — GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1 mini

slides.title: Turn-Based Voice Feels Like a Walkie-Talkie
slides.body: Advanced Voice Mode waited for the user to finish speaking, then generated a full response before speaking back — no real interruption, no natural overlap, no acknowledgment while listening.
bullets: Users can't interrupt mid-response the way they would with a person
No backchannel cues ('mm-hmm') while the model is listening
Latency between 'user stops talking' and 'model starts talking' breaks the illusion of a live conversation

slides.title: A Model That Decides to Speak, Listen, or Interrupt Many Times a Second
slides.body: GPT-Live's full-duplex architecture continuously decides — many times per second — whether to speak, listen, pause, acknowledge, interrupt, or invoke a tool, rather than alternating strict turns.
bullets: Runs as a native audio-in, audio-out model, not a speech-to-text-to-LLM-to-speech pipeline
Can be interrupted mid-sentence and adjust or stop instead of finishing a queued response
For requests beyond its native capability — complex math, multi-step research, tool use — it hands off live to GPT-5.5 running in parallel, then speaks the result

slides.title: GPT-Live-1 vs. Advanced Voice Mode, on OpenAI's Own Benchmarks
Two Sizes, Two Tiers
slides.body: GPT-Live-1 becomes the default voice model for ChatGPT Go, Plus, and Pro subscribers; GPT-Live-1 mini serves free-tier users.
bullets: Both roll out across iOS, Android, and web
The 'mini' tier trades some capability for lower latency/cost at free-tier scale
The handoff to GPT-5.5 is what lets a comparatively fast voice model still answer hard, tool-requiring questions

slides.title: Worked Example: Asking It to Research Something Mid-Conversation
bullets: You're mid-conversation and ask GPT-Live a question that needs a live web lookup
Instead of stalling or guessing, GPT-Live recognizes the request exceeds native capability and hands off to GPT-5.5 in parallel
GPT-5.5 runs the multi-step search/tool-use work while GPT-Live keeps the conversation alive rather than going silent
GPT-Live speaks the synthesized result back once GPT-5.5 returns it — the handoff is largely invisible to the user

slides.title: Where Full-Duplex Voice Still Trips Up
slides.body: Early users flagged the model as occasionally over-eager to interject.
bullets: Reports of 'over-enthusiasm' — jumping in when the user was still mid-thought, not actually pausing
Full-duplex is a genuinely harder turn-taking problem than turn-based voice; getting the timing of when to speak right is as hard as generating good content
Not a fit for scenarios needing strict, auditable turn boundaries (e.g. structured intake calls) where interruption behavior needs to stay fully predictable

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: GPT-Live replaces ChatGPT's turn-based voice mode with a native full-duplex model that can be interrupted mid-response
It nearly doubles GPQA accuracy (45.3% -> 84.2%) and jumps BrowseComp from 0.7% to 75.2% versus the previous voice mode, by handing hard requests to GPT-5.5 in parallel
Two tiers ship: GPT-Live-1 for paid plans, GPT-Live-1 mini for free-tier, across iOS/Android/web
The tradeoff for natural interruption is a genuinely hard turn-taking problem — early users report it sometimes interjects too eagerly

questions.prompt: What does 'full-duplex' mean in the context of GPT-Live's architecture?
options: It runs two separate models and picks the better answer
It processes incoming speech and generates outgoing speech at the same time, rather than strict turns
It only works over a duplex network connection
It doubles the context window size
questions.explanation: Full-duplex means the model listens and speaks concurrently — deciding many times a second whether to talk, listen, pause, or interrupt — instead of waiting for the user to finish before generating a full response.

questions.prompt: How does GPT-Live handle a request that exceeds its native voice capability, like multi-step research?
options: It refuses and asks the user to type instead
It hands off to GPT-5.5 running in parallel, then speaks the synthesized result
It always answers with its best guess without any handoff
It switches the user to text-only mode automatically
questions.explanation: GPT-Live recognizes when a request needs more than native voice reasoning and delegates to GPT-5.5 running in parallel, keeping the conversation alive while it works, then voices the result.

questions.prompt: On OpenAI's benchmarks, roughly how much did GPT-Live-1 (High reasoning) improve over Advanced Voice Mode on BrowseComp?
options: A small, roughly 5-point bump
From 0.7% to 75.2%, driven by the handoff to a full reasoning model for agentic search
It scored slightly worse due to added voice latency
BrowseComp wasn't run on either model
questions.explanation: BrowseComp tests agentic web search. Advanced Voice Mode essentially couldn't do this in-voice (0.7%); GPT-Live's ability to hand tool-heavy work to GPT-5.5 pushed that to 75.2%.

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: The Server Asks, the User Answers
posts.subtitle: The primitive that lets a server pause mid-call and request exactly the input it's missing.
posts.summary: Elicitation lets an MCP server pause a tool call and send the client a JSON-Schema-described question, so the human — not the model — supplies the missing piece. Responses come back as accept, decline, or cancel, and the spec deliberately restricts schemas to flat primitive fields and bans requesting sensitive data through the channel.

slides.title: A Tool Call That Stops and Asks a Question
slides.body: MCP elicitation lets a server pause mid-operation and request structured input directly from the human, through the client — no model guessing required.

slides.title: Before Elicitation, a Server Could Only Fail or Guess
bullets: A deploy tool needs a target environment name the model never provided; a booking server needs a date the user forgot to mention; a destructive action needs explicit confirmation.

Without a way to ask, the server had three bad options: fail with an error and make the model re-guess, silently pick a default, or require every parameter to be configured up front at connection time.
Any of those breaks the moment a workflow is genuinely interactive — the missing piece lives in the human's head, not in the conversation so far.

slides.title: elicitation/create Sends a Schema, Not Free Text
bullets: A client that supports the feature declares an `elicitation` capability at initialization; a server can then send an `elicitation/create` request mid-call with a human-readable `message` and a `requestedSchema`.

That schema is deliberately restricted to a flat object of primitive properties only — strings, numbers, booleans, enums — with constraints like minLength or format: email. No nested objects, no arrays of objects.
The client renders that schema as an actual form (or CLI prompt) instead of just piping text back to the model, so the human fills in exactly the fields the server asked for.

slides.title: Three Outcomes, Not Two: Accept, Decline, Cancel
bullets: accept: the user explicitly submitted data — the response carries a content object matching the requested schema.
decline: the user explicitly refused the request — content is omitted, and the server should treat this as a real 'no', not a retry-able failure.
cancel: the user dismissed the dialog without choosing — content is omitted, and the server should treat this as inconclusive rather than a refusal.
The spec calls this out on purpose: humans get distracted, close dialogs, or come back later, and collapsing that into a boolean would lose information a well-behaved server actually needs.

slides.title: A CI Tool Confirms Before It Deletes a Branch
bullets: The model calls a `cleanup_stale_branches` tool. The server finds 14 branches untouched for 90+ days but has no idea if that threshold or that exact list is what the user actually wants.

Instead of deleting them or asking the model to re-prompt the user in chat, the server sends elicitation/create with a schema: a boolean `confirm` field and a number `days_threshold` field, plus a message listing the 14 branch names.

The client shows a real form. The user changes the threshold to 120 days and confirms — the server gets back `{action: "accept", content: {confirm: true, days_threshold: 120}}` and re-runs its own query with the corrected value, not a value the model invented.

slides.title: Elicitation vs. the Other MCP Primitives
bullets: Elicitation is the only primitive where the payload is a question for a human, not context for the model or a scope declaration.

rows: Server asks the human a direct, schema-shaped question
Server borrows the client's LLM to reason
Client tells server which directories are in scope
Model invokes a server function with args it already has

slides.title: The Restrictions Are the Point, Not a Limitation
bullets: The spec explicitly bans using elicitation to request sensitive information — passwords, API keys, credit card numbers have no business flowing through a form a server designed.

Flat-primitives-only isn't laziness: it keeps every client able to render a generic form without a bespoke UI per server, and stops elicitation from becoming a way to smuggle arbitrary structured data collection into a tool call.

Skip elicitation for anything the model can already infer from context, and for genuinely sensitive input — route those through the client's own auth flow instead. Reach for it when the missing piece is a fact, choice, or confirmation only the human has.

slides.title: A Form, Not a Chat Message
bullets: Elicitation gives a server a structured way to ask the human directly — mid-call — instead of failing, guessing, or offloading the question to the model.
Three response actions (accept / decline / cancel) preserve the difference between 'no' and 'not now,' which a server should handle differently.
Schemas are intentionally flat and primitive-only, and sensitive data is explicitly off-limits — the constraints exist to keep the channel safe and every client able to render it generically.

questions.prompt: What does a server send when it calls elicitation/create?
options: A raw text prompt for the model to answer on the user's behalf
A message plus a requestedSchema describing the structured input it needs
An OAuth token request
The full list of the client's declared roots
questions.explanation: elicitation/create carries a human-readable message and a requestedSchema (a restricted JSON Schema), which the client renders as a form for the human to fill in directly.

questions.prompt: Why does MCP elicitation use three response actions (accept, decline, cancel) instead of just success/failure?
options: To match HTTP status code conventions
Because decline (an explicit 'no') and cancel (dismissed without choosing) need different handling from a well-behaved server
It's a legacy artifact from an earlier protocol version
Because JSON-RPC requires exactly three response types
questions.explanation: A user explicitly declining is a real answer a server should respect; a user dismissing the dialog without choosing is inconclusive. Collapsing both into one 'failure' state would lose that distinction.

questions.prompt: Why are elicitation schemas restricted to flat objects with primitive properties only?
options: JSON Schema doesn't support nested objects at all
To keep every client able to render a generic form and to discourage using elicitation as a general-purpose data collection channel
Because nested schemas are too slow to parse
Because the MCP spec forbids servers from using enums
questions.explanation: Flat, primitive-only schemas mean any compliant client can render a sensible form without server-specific UI, and the constraint keeps elicitation scoped to quick, well-defined questions rather than arbitrary structured input.

posts.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Who Talks to Whom
posts.subtitle: Supervisor, pipeline, and swarm patterns — and the coordination tax each one charges.
posts.summary: Splitting a task across multiple LLM agents can cut context bloat and specialize behavior, but only if the coordination pattern fits the task. This post breaks down the three dominant multi-agent orchestration patterns — supervisor/worker, sequential pipeline, and decentralized swarm — with the concrete cost and failure tradeoffs of each.

slides.title: When One Agent Runs Out of Role
slides.body: A single agent juggling planning, coding, and reviewing tends to blur all three into mediocre output. Multi-agent orchestration splits the job across specialized agents — but the wiring between them decides whether that split helps or just multiplies cost.
bullets: Three dominant patterns: supervisor/worker, sequential pipeline, decentralized swarm
Every pattern trades coordination overhead for specialization
The wrong pattern for a simple task can cost 3-5x the tokens of one agent

slides.title: One Context Window, Too Many Jobs
slides.body: Stuff planning, tool use, self-critique, and long-term memory into one system prompt and each instruction competes for the model's attention.
bullets: A single agent's system prompt grows every time you add a responsibility
Role conflation: the same agent that wrote the code is asked to judge it, so it rarely catches its own mistakes
No natural checkpoint to inject human review or swap in a cheaper model for a simpler sub-step

slides.title: Split the Role, Not Just the Prompt
slides.body: Orchestration means one thing calls other agents like tools and decides what happens with what they return. The three shapes below differ in who holds that decision.
bullets: Supervisor/worker: one orchestrator agent routes each sub-task to a specialist and merges results
Sequential pipeline: fixed order, each agent's output is the next agent's entire input
Swarm (handoff): agents pass control directly to each other, no fixed center

slides.title: Three Shapes, Three Failure Modes
bullets: Supervisor/worker: a router agent picks the next specialist based on shared state — flexible, but the supervisor becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck
Sequential pipeline: Planner -> Coder -> Reviewer -> Tester, each stage strictly gated on the last — predictable, but one bad handoff (a vague plan) poisons every stage after it
Swarm/handoff: any agent can transfer control to any other agent it knows about — cheap to add new agents, but nothing enforces that the whole thing terminates

slides.title: Worked Example: A Code-Review Agent Team
slides.body: A supervisor gets 'fix this failing test.' It doesn't fix anything itself — it only decides who acts next.
bullets: Supervisor reads the failure, calls a Diagnose agent with just the stack trace, not the whole repo
Diagnose agent returns a 3-line root-cause summary; supervisor passes that summary plus the one relevant file to a Patch agent
Patch agent proposes a diff; supervisor calls a Test agent to run it in a sandbox before ever showing the user
Total: 4 focused LLM calls with small contexts, versus 1 call carrying the entire repo diff, stack trace, and test output at once

slides.title: Picking a Pattern

rows: Dynamic routing when the right specialist isn't known in advance
Supervisor becomes the bottleneck and single point of failure
One bad stage output corrupts everything downstream
Open-ended tasks where the next best agent isn't fixed
No built-in termination check; can loop or hand off indefinitely

slides.title: The Coordination Tax
slides.body: Every extra agent hop is a full extra LLM call, and most of what it reads is a summary of what already happened, not new information.
bullets: N agents on one task means roughly N separate context windows and N latencies stacked, not parallel — cost and time both compound
Compounding error: if each agent stage is 90% reliable, a 4-stage sequential chain is only about 66% reliable end-to-end (0.9^4 ≈ 0.656)
Skip orchestration for tasks a single well-scoped prompt already handles well — the fix for a bad single-agent prompt is usually a better prompt, not more agents
Add a supervisor only once there are 3+ genuinely different specialist roles; two agents rarely need a third to referee them

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Multi-agent orchestration splits responsibility, it does not reduce total work — budget for roughly N times the tokens and latency of a single call
Supervisor/worker fits dynamic routing; sequential pipeline fits known multi-step processes; swarm fits open-ended handoffs
Compounding reliability is the hidden cost: chain enough 90%-reliable agents and the system-wide success rate drags below 70%
Default to one well-scoped agent; reach for orchestration only when there are genuinely distinct specialist roles that benefit from separate context

questions.prompt: In the supervisor/worker pattern, what is the supervisor's main job?
options: Executing every sub-task itself for consistency
Deciding which specialist agent handles the next step and merging results
Storing the long-term memory for all agents
Running the final unit tests
questions.explanation: The supervisor doesn't do the specialist work — it routes state to the right worker and decides what happens with what comes back. That routing role is also why it becomes the bottleneck: every decision passes through it.

questions.prompt: Why can a 4-stage sequential pipeline where each stage is 90% reliable end up below 70% reliable overall?
options: Because agents run out of context window
Because each stage's success is conditional on all previous stages succeeding, so probabilities multiply (0.9^4 ≈ 65.6%)
Because sequential pipelines always use a slower model
Because token limits force truncation after 3 agents
questions.explanation: Independent-stage reliabilities multiply in a strict sequential chain: 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 ≈ 0.656. A single bad handoff early in the chain poisons everything after it.

questions.prompt: A task can already be handled reliably by one well-scoped agent with a focused prompt. What's the right call?
options: Add a supervisor and two workers anyway, for future flexibility
Split it into a swarm so agents can hand off as needed
Keep it as one agent — orchestration adds cost and failure surface without a corresponding benefit here
Always use a sequential pipeline for consistency across the codebase
questions.explanation: Orchestration overhead — extra tokens, extra latency, compounding failure — is only worth paying when there are genuinely distinct specialist roles. A task one agent already handles well doesn't need more agents.

posts.title: Kimi K3: Moonshot's 2.8T Open-Weight Flagship
posts.subtitle: 896 experts, 16 fire per token, 1M-token context — and the full checkpoint is public.
posts.summary: Moonshot AI open-weighted Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model that activates only 104B parameters per token via 896 routed experts. It ships a native 1M-token context, a built-in MoonViT-V2 vision encoder, and MXFP4/MXFP8 quantization-aware weights — but serving the full checkpoint still needs a multi-GPU cluster.

slides.title: A 2.8-Trillion-Parameter Model, Fully Open
slides.body: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3's weights publicly — the largest open-weight model shipped to date, built as a sparse Mixture-of-Experts network rather than a dense giant.
bullets: 2.8T total parameters, only 104B activated per token
896 routed experts + 2 shared experts, 16 selected per token
Weights and code public under the Kimi K3 License

slides.title: Frontier-Tier Usually Means Closed-Weight
slides.body: The most capable models are almost all API-only. Open-weight releases have historically traded capability for openness.
bullets: Fable 5, Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.6 all ship as closed APIs, not downloadable weights
Prior open models stayed smaller to stay servable on modest hardware
A trillion-plus-parameter dense model would be too expensive to even run, let alone open-source

slides.title: Sparsity Is the Trick: 16 of 896 Experts Fire
slides.body: K3's Stable LatentMoE framework keeps almost all weights dormant on any given token, so compute scales with the 104B active slice, not the 2.8T total.
bullets: 93 layers total: 69 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers + 24 Gated Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) layers
Attention Residuals (AttnRes) stabilize training at this depth and sparsity
Native MXFP4 weights with MXFP8 activations via quantization-aware training, not post-hoc quantization

slides.title: One Encoder for Text, Image, and Video
slides.body: Multimodal input doesn't go through a bolted-on adapter — it's a native part of the model.
bullets: MoonViT-V2 vision encoder: 401M parameters, trained jointly with the language model
160K-token vocabulary
1,048,576-token context window (1M), enough for a large codebase or a long video transcript in one pass

slides.title: The Spec Sheet
What 1M Tokens Actually Buys You
slides.body: A concrete case: feeding K3 an entire mid-sized codebase plus its issue tracker history in one context window.
bullets: No manual chunking or retrieval step needed to fit the repo in context
The model can trace a bug across files it read directly, not summaries of files
Same context budget covers a multi-hour video transcript via the native vision/video path

slides.title: Open Weights ≠ Runs on a Laptop
slides.body: Sparsity cuts compute per token, not storage. The full 2.8T-parameter checkpoint still has to live somewhere.
bullets: Serving K3 needs vLLM, SGLang, or Moonshot's own TokenSpeed engine across multiple GPUs/nodes
Even MXFP4-quantized, a 2.8T-parameter checkpoint is a multi-hundred-gigabyte download and load
The 'Kimi K3 License' is Moonshot's own terms, not a standard OSI license — read it before commercial use
For most teams, the hosted API at platform.kimi.ai is the practical entry point, not self-hosting

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: 2.8T total / 104B active MoE, 896 experts with 16 selected per token — sparsity, not size, drives efficiency
1M-token context plus a native MoonViT-V2 encoder for text, image, and video in one model
Moonshot reports ~2.5× overall scaling efficiency versus Kimi K2
Weights are public, but serving the full checkpoint still needs multi-GPU infrastructure
License is custom ('Kimi K3 License') — check terms before commercial deployment

questions.prompt: How many of Kimi K3's 896 routed experts activate for a given token?
options: All 896
questions.explanation: 16 of 896 routed experts (plus 2 shared experts) fire per token. That sparsity is why only 104B of the 2.8T total parameters are activated per forward pass, cutting compute far below what a dense model of the same size would need.

questions.prompt: What lets Kimi K3 process images and video without a separate pipeline?
options: A bolt-on OCR plugin called after generation
The native MoonViT-V2 vision encoder trained as part of the model
Converting every image to a text caption before inference
It doesn't support images
questions.explanation: MoonViT-V2 (401M parameters) is built into K3 itself, so the model handles text, images, and video natively rather than routing through an external adapter.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't K3's open-weight release mean it can run on a single consumer GPU?
options: Because the license forbids local deployment
Because the full 2.8T-parameter checkpoint must still be stored and served, typically across multiple GPUs or nodes, even though only 104B parameters activate per token
Because it has no quantized version available
Because it only supports TPU hardware
questions.explanation: MoE sparsity reduces compute per token, not the memory needed to hold the model. Engines like vLLM and SGLang still have to load the entire 2.8T-parameter checkpoint — even in MXFP4 — across a multi-GPU cluster.

posts.title: GraphRAG: Retrieval Over a Graph, Not Just Chunks
posts.subtitle: When the question needs the shape of the whole dataset, nearest-neighbor chunks can't answer it.
posts.summary: GraphRAG extracts an LLM-generated knowledge graph from a corpus, clusters it into hierarchical communities, and pre-summarizes each one. That lets it answer whole-dataset questions ('what are the top themes here?') that plain vector RAG's nearest-neighbor chunk retrieval structurally can't reach — at the cost of a real upfront indexing pass.

slides.title: When Vector Search Can't See the Forest
slides.body: Standard RAG retrieves the chunks nearest to a query embedding. GraphRAG instead builds a knowledge graph from the corpus and reasons over its structure.
bullets: Built by Microsoft Research for questions that span an entire private dataset
Trades a real indexing cost for answers no single chunk contains
Open-sourced pipeline, 20K+ GitHub stars since its 2024 release

slides.title: 'Top 5 Themes' Isn't in Any One Chunk
slides.body: Top-k similarity search finds text that looks like the query — not text that summarizes the whole corpus.
bullets: Entity-focused queries ('What is Novorossiya?') work fine with plain vector RAG
Dataset-wide queries ('What are the top 5 themes in this dataset?') have no single matching chunk
Answering them requires aggregating across the entire corpus, which nearest-neighbor retrieval isn't built to do

slides.title: Extract a Graph, Then Summarize It Hierarchically
slides.body: GraphRAG's indexing pipeline runs once per corpus, before any query arrives.
bullets: 1. An LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities and relationships into a graph
2. The graph is broken into hierarchical communities via bottom-up clustering (Microsoft's graspologic library)
3. An LLM pre-generates a summary for every community, at every level of the hierarchy
4. At query time, the question is routed to global or local search over these pre-built structures

slides.title: Global Search vs. Local (DRIFT) Search
slides.body: The two query types hit completely different parts of the index.
bullets: Global search: map-reduce over community summaries — for holistic questions like 'catch me up on the last two weeks'
Local/DRIFT search: walks the entity neighborhood around specific nodes — for precise, entity-focused questions
Picking the wrong mode either wastes tokens scanning irrelevant summaries or misses the aggregate answer entirely

slides.title: Dynamic Community Selection: Real Numbers
slides.body: Microsoft Research measured what pruning irrelevant communities before the expensive map-reduce step actually costs and buys.

rows: +34% cost, but 58.8%/60.0% win rate on comprehensiveness/empowerment

slides.title: A Support Ticket Corpus, Two Ways
slides.body: Query: "What are the top recurring themes in last quarter's tickets?"
bullets: Vector RAG: returns a handful of tickets whose embeddings are closest to the query — none of them individually describes an aggregate theme
GraphRAG: entities like 'login flow', 'billing', 'mobile crash' were already extracted and clustered into a 'product areas' community during indexing
The LLM answers by combining a few pre-written community summaries instead of skimming thousands of raw tickets

slides.title: Tradeoffs and Takeaways
slides.body: The indexing pass is the real cost: an LLM call per chunk to extract entities, then more calls to summarize every community at every level — paid upfront, unlike vector RAG's cheap one-time embedding step.
bullets: Worth it for corpora queried repeatedly where dataset-wide questions matter (research libraries, internal wikis) — overkill for a single-document Q&A bot
Graph quality depends entirely on how well the LLM extracts entities; bad extraction means a bad graph
Dynamic community selection cut global-search token cost 77% with no quality loss at shallow depth (Microsoft Research)
GraphRAG complements local/vector search via DRIFT mode — it doesn't replace it

questions.prompt: Why does plain vector RAG struggle with a question like 'what are the top 5 themes in this dataset'?
options: Embeddings can't be computed for long documents
No single chunk contains an aggregate answer across the whole corpus — nearest-neighbor retrieval only finds locally similar text
Vector databases can't store more than a few thousand chunks
LLMs can't read more than one retrieved chunk at a time
questions.explanation: Top-k similarity search finds chunks that look like the query, not chunks that summarize the whole dataset. Global questions need aggregation across the corpus, which is exactly what GraphRAG's pre-built community summaries provide.

questions.prompt: In GraphRAG, what does a 'community' represent?
options: A single source document
A cluster of related entities in the extracted knowledge graph, grouped hierarchically
A group of users who asked similar questions
A shard of the vector index
questions.explanation: After extracting entities and relationships into a graph, GraphRAG runs bottom-up clustering to group related entities into communities at multiple hierarchy levels, then pre-summarizes each one.

questions.prompt: Per Microsoft Research's measurements, what did dynamic community selection achieve at search-depth level 1 versus static global search?
options: 34% higher cost for better quality
77% lower token cost with no drop in quality
A completely different knowledge graph structure
No measurable difference in cost or quality
questions.explanation: By rating community relevance top-down and pruning irrelevant branches before the expensive map-reduce step, dynamic selection cut community reports processed from ~1,500 to ~470 — a 77% token-cost reduction — while matching static search's quality at that depth.
