posts.title: Tool Calling: How an LLM Actually Triggers a Function
posts.subtitle: The model never runs code — it emits structured JSON and a host process does the rest
posts.summary: Tool calling isn't the model reaching out and running code — it's the model emitting a structured JSON object that matches a schema you declared, which a host process intercepts, executes, and feeds back as a new message. The reliability comes from constrained decoding and a strict request/response loop, not from the model being smarter about APIs.

slides.title: The Model Never Touches a Single API
slides.body: Every 'agent calling a tool' is really the model predicting text that happens to look like a function call, and a separate program deciding to act on it.

slides.title: Free-Form Text Is a Terrible Interface for Actions
bullets: Early 'agents' asked the model to write prose like 'I should search for the weather in Austin' and then regex-parsed it — brittle, and one phrasing drift breaks the parser.
A model has no way to actually execute anything; it only predicts the next token. Without a strict contract, arguments come back malformed, quoted inconsistently, or with invented parameter names.
Hallucinated tools are the real risk: given no explicit list, a model will confidently invoke an API that doesn't exist, because 'a function that does X' is a plausible completion.

slides.title: You Declare a JSON Schema; the Model Fills It In
slides.body: Modern tool calling puts a machine-readable spec — name, description, and a JSON Schema for the arguments — into the request. The model is trained (and often decoding-constrained) to emit output matching that schema instead of prose whenever a tool fits.
bullets: The runtime, not the model, executes the call: it validates the JSON against the schema, runs the real function, and appends the result as a new 'tool' message in the conversation.
Constrained/grammar decoding masks out tokens that would produce invalid JSON at each step, so malformed output becomes a token-sampling impossibility rather than a hope.
The model only ever sees text: the tool definition going in, and the tool's result coming back as another message it reads like any other context.

slides.title: It's a Loop, Not a Single Call
bullets: 1) User message goes in with the list of available tools. 2) Model emits either a normal reply or a tool_call (name + JSON arguments). 3) Host executes it and appends a tool-result message. 4) Model resumes with that result in context — often producing another tool_call before ever answering.

Independent calls can run in parallel: if the model requests two tools with no data dependency between them, most runtimes fire both and merge the results back in before the next model turn — cutting round-trip latency roughly in half for that step.
Each round trip costs a full model inference pass, so a 4-tool-call chain isn't 'one request' — it's five: four tool turns plus the final synthesis.

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Independent Lookups
slides.body: Prompt: 'What's the weather in Austin, and what's 50 USD in EUR?' — two unrelated facts, so a well-built agent fires both tools in parallel rather than sequentially.
bullets: Turn 1 — model output: two tool_calls in the same message: get_weather({"city":"Austin"}) and convert_currency({"amount":50,"from":"USD","to":"EUR"}).
Host executes both concurrently, gets back {"tempF":91,"conditions":"sunny"} and {"result":46.10}, and appends both as tool-result messages tagged with matching call IDs.
Turn 2 — model reads both results in context and writes the final prose answer: 'It's 91°F and sunny in Austin; 50 USD is about €46.10.' No new tool calls needed.

slides.title: Prompted Parsing vs. Native Tool Calling

rows: Ad-hoc text pattern in the prompt
Structured field the API returns directly
Silently mis-parsed or crashes the parser
Rare — one action per text turn
Multiple tool_calls in a single turn
Standardized across most major model APIs

slides.title: Where It Still Breaks
bullets: Tool-selection accuracy degrades as the toolbox grows — past roughly a few dozen simultaneously offered tools, models start picking the wrong one or missing the right one, even with perfect schemas. Curate the set per-task instead of exposing everything at once.

A schema only constrains shape, not truth: the model can still fill valid JSON with a hallucinated argument value (a city that doesn't exist, an ID it invented), so the executing function still has to validate semantically.

Tool calling has no built-in permission model — anything declared as a tool is something the model will eventually try to call. Destructive tools (delete, send, pay) need an explicit confirmation step outside the loop, not just a well-worded description.

Don't reach for tool calling when the answer is already in the model's context or training knowledge — every call adds a full inference round trip's worth of latency and cost for something a direct answer would've solved instantly.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Tool calling = a JSON contract + constrained decoding + a host loop — the model still only predicts text, it never executes anything itself.
Independent tool calls can and should run in parallel; dependent ones force sequential round trips, each costing a full inference pass.
A valid schema guarantees well-formed arguments, not correct ones — always validate values, not just shape, before executing.
More tools isn't free: curate the offered set per task rather than exposing your entire API surface at once.

questions.prompt: What actually makes modern tool calling more reliable than the old 'parse the model's prose' approach?
options: The model has been given direct code-execution access
A declared JSON Schema plus decoding constraints that make invalid output impossible to sample
A bigger context window so the model remembers the API docs better
The model is fine-tuned on that specific company's API
questions.explanation: Reliability comes from the contract (schema) and the decoding-time constraint that masks out tokens which would break it — not from the model becoming smarter about APIs or gaining any real execution ability.

questions.prompt: In the weather + currency example, why do both tool calls happen in the same turn instead of one after another?
options: The model can only ever emit one tool call, so this is actually two separate turns
The two calls are independent of each other's output, so the host can execute them concurrently before the next model turn
Parallel calls are required by the JSON Schema spec
It's cheaper to always batch every tool call regardless of dependency
questions.explanation: Parallel execution is only safe when calls don't depend on each other's results. If converting currency needed the weather result first, they'd have to run sequentially across separate turns.

questions.prompt: A team keeps adding tools to their agent — it's now offered 60 tools on every request — and accuracy is dropping. What's the most likely cause?
options: JSON Schema validation stops working above a fixed tool count
Tool-selection accuracy degrades as the offered set grows, even when every schema is well-formed
The model runs out of context space to store 60 JSON schemas
Parallel tool calling gets disabled automatically above 50 tools
questions.explanation: This is a selection problem, not a formatting one — schemas can be perfectly valid and the model still picks the wrong tool or misses the right one as the candidate list grows. The fix is curating a smaller, task-relevant tool set, not fixing the schemas.

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: Splitting the Difference on KV Cache
posts.subtitle: Why Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B don't give every attention head its own keys and values
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shrinks the KV cache by clustering query heads into groups that each share a single key/value head, trading a small amount of representational capacity for a large cut in inference memory. It's the attention variant actually shipping in Llama 2's larger models and Mistral 7B, not just a research idea.

slides.title: Every Attention Head Used to Get Its Own Keys and Values
slides.body: Multi-head attention gives each head an independent key and value projection. That's expressive — and it's also the reason the KV cache eats so much memory during inference.

slides.title: The KV Cache Grows With Every Head, Every Token
bullets: During autoregressive generation, the model caches a key and value vector per head per token so it never recomputes them. With H heads, that cache is H times bigger than a single-head model's — and it keeps growing linearly with sequence length on top of that.
A 70B-class model with 64 attention heads stores 64 separate key/value pairs per token, per layer — across 80 layers that adds up fast, especially at long context lengths.

Multi-Query Attention (MQA) is the extreme fix: collapse all heads down to ONE shared key/value head. Memory savings are dramatic, but quality can suffer because every query head is now reading from the same compressed key/value space.

slides.title: GQA Groups Heads Instead of Sharing One K/V for All of Them
slides.body: Grouped-Query Attention splits the query heads into G groups. Every query head keeps its own projection, but all heads inside a group share one key head and one value head. G = H recovers standard multi-head attention; G = 1 recovers MQA. GQA picks a middle value of G.
bullets: Fewer distinct key/value projections to store means a smaller KV cache — roughly H/G times smaller than full multi-head attention.
Existing MHA checkpoints can be 'uptrained' into GQA by mean-pooling each group's original key/value heads into one shared head, then fine-tuning briefly — no need to pretrain from scratch.
Because most of the architecture is unchanged, GQA models train and behave almost like standard transformers, just with a cheaper cache to carry at inference time.

slides.title: The Query-to-KV-Head Ratio Is a Tunable Knob
slides.body: The group size G is a design choice made per model, usually picked so it divides evenly into the total head count.
bullets: MHA: G = H (e.g. 64 query heads → 64 KV heads) — maximum quality, maximum cache size.
GQA: 1 < G < H (e.g. 64 query heads grouped down to 8 KV heads) — the middle ground most production models actually ship.
MQA: G = 1 (all query heads → a single shared KV head) — minimum cache, biggest quality risk.

slides.title: Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B Both Ship With GQA
bullets: Llama 2 70B: 64 attention heads grouped down to 8 KV heads — roughly an 8x smaller KV cache than full MHA would need at that same head count.
Mistral 7B: 32 attention heads grouped down to 8 KV heads — a 4x reduction, part of what let it run efficiently on more modest hardware.
Meta kept standard MHA on the smaller Llama 2 variants (7B, 13B) — GQA's payoff is biggest where the cache is biggest: larger models and longer contexts.

slides.title: Cache Size vs. Quality: Where Each Variant Lands
GQA Isn't Free, and It Isn't Always the Right Call
slides.body: The savings are real, but they come with caveats worth knowing before reaching for GQA.
bullets: Converting a pretrained MHA model to GQA needs an uptraining pass — skipping it and just deleting KV heads outright tanks quality instead of gracefully trading it off.
Very small models rarely bother: when the KV cache isn't your inference bottleneck, GQA adds architectural complexity for little practical gain.
The group count G is a fixed choice baked in at training time — unlike batch size or context length, you can't tune it per request after the model is trained.

GQA doesn't reduce weight count or FLOPs per token the way something like Mixture of Experts does — it specifically targets the inference-time KV cache, so pair it with quantization or PagedAttention for compounding savings rather than expecting it to solve everything alone.

slides.title: The Core Idea in One Line
bullets: KV cache size scales with the number of distinct key/value heads, not the number of query heads.
GQA groups query heads so they share key/value heads, landing between full MHA and single-head MQA on the memory-vs-quality spectrum.
Real models use it today: Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B both ship GQA with 8 KV heads in production, not just as a research technique.
It's an inference-memory optimization, not a capacity optimization — combine it with other efficiency techniques rather than treating it as a complete solution.

questions.prompt: In Grouped-Query Attention, what do the query heads within one group share?
options: Their own separate query projections
A single key projection and a single value projection
The final output projection only
The positional embeddings for the sequence
questions.explanation: Every query head keeps its own query projection — what's shared within a group is one key projection and one value projection. That's the whole mechanism: fewer distinct K/V projections to cache, while queries stay fully independent.

questions.prompt: Llama 2 70B uses GQA with 64 query heads grouped into 8 KV heads. Roughly how much smaller is its KV cache versus full multi-head attention at that same head count?
options: About 2x smaller
About 8x smaller
About 64x smaller
No smaller — GQA doesn't change cache size
questions.explanation: Cache size scales with the number of distinct KV heads, not query heads. 64 query heads grouped into 8 shared KV heads means roughly an 8x reduction in key/value storage compared to giving all 64 heads their own KV pair.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of pushing all the way to Multi-Query Attention (a single shared KV head for every query head)?
options: Training becomes numerically unstable
The model can no longer be used for autoregressive generation
Quality can degrade because too much key/value information is compressed into one shared representation
Positional encoding stops working correctly
questions.explanation: MQA gets the biggest memory win by collapsing every query head down to one shared KV head, but that squeezes all of the model's key/value representational capacity into a single space — which can hurt output quality. GQA exists specifically to interpolate between that extreme and full multi-head attention.

posts.title: Late Interaction: Retrieval That Keeps Every Token's Vote
posts.subtitle: Bi-encoders squash a document into one vector; cross-encoders read every token pair but can't be precomputed. ColBERT's MaxSim gets both.
posts.summary: Late interaction retrieval (introduced by ColBERT) encodes queries and documents into per-token embedding matrices instead of single vectors, then scores relevance with MaxSim: each query token finds its best-matching document token, and those maxes get summed. It recovers most of a cross-encoder's fine-grained matching quality while still letting document representations be computed and indexed offline — at the cost of storing many vectors per document instead of one.

slides.title: One Vector Per Document Is a Compression You're Paying For
slides.body: Every dense retriever squashes a document down to a single point in embedding space. Late interaction asks: what if you didn't have to?

slides.title: Bi-Encoders Are Fast Because They Forget
bullets: A standard dense retriever (bi-encoder) runs the query and each document through an encoder separately, then pools all their tokens into ONE vector each — relevance is just a dot product between two points.

That single vector has to represent every entity, number, and rare term in the whole document at once. A query for an exact SKU, error code, or proper noun can get diluted into a generic semantic neighborhood and lose the match.

Cross-encoders fix this by concatenating query+document and running full self-attention so every query token can attend to every document token directly — much higher quality, but the score can't be computed until BOTH texts are known.

That makes cross-encoders unusable as a first-stage retriever over millions of documents: you can't precompute anything, so you'd need one full transformer forward pass per query-document pair. In practice they only rerank a small shortlist a cheaper retriever already produced.

slides.title: Keep One Vector Per Token, Not Per Document
bullets: Late interaction (ColBERT, Khattab & Zaharia) encodes the query and the document independently — same as a bi-encoder — but skips the pooling step. Each token keeps its own small vector, so a document becomes a MATRIX of embeddings, not a single point.

Because the document side is still encoded independently of the query, every document's token matrix can be computed once, offline, and stored in an index — the expensive transformer pass never has to wait for a query.

At query time you only run the (short) query through the encoder and then do a lightweight comparison against the precomputed document matrices — no second transformer pass over the document is needed.

This is the 'late' in late interaction: the two sides interact only at the final scoring step, after both have already been independently embedded — as opposed to a cross-encoder's 'early' interaction inside the transformer itself.

slides.title: MaxSim: Every Query Token Picks Its Best Match
slides.body: For each query token embedding, find its single highest-similarity token anywhere in the document, then sum those maxes across all query tokens.
bullets: score(Q, D) = Σ over query tokens q of [ max over document tokens d of (q · d) ] — each query token independently finds whichever document token it matches best, then those per-token maxima are added up.

This gives the model soft, per-term matching: a query token for an exact identifier can still find and reward an exact match buried anywhere in the document, instead of that signal being averaged away into one pooled vector.
It's still cheap relative to a cross-encoder: MaxSim is just a matrix multiply plus a max and a sum — no additional transformer layers run at query time.

Because the operation is a similarity matrix over two small sets of vectors, it composes naturally with approximate pruning: you don't have to compare a query against every token of every document to get a good score estimate.

slides.title: A Query That a Bi-Encoder Would Blur
bullets: Query: 'rollback procedure for error E4021'. A pooled bi-encoder vector for this query mixes 'rollback', 'procedure', and the specific code E4021 into one averaged direction — a document that's strong on 'rollback procedure' but never mentions E4021 can still score high.

With late interaction, the query keeps a separate vector for the E4021 token. That vector's MaxSim term can only score high against a document token that's actually close to E4021 — a near-exact match in the index, not a generic semantic neighborhood.

Meanwhile 'rollback' and 'procedure' still get their own MaxSim terms and can match paraphrases like 'revert steps' via semantic similarity — you keep soft matching on the descriptive words and sharp matching on the identifier, in the same score.
The final score is the sum of both kinds of evidence in one pass — no separate keyword-search (BM25) system needed to catch what the dense vector missed.

slides.title: Three Ways to Score Relevance
bullets: The core tradeoff is exactly where interaction happens: never (bi-encoder), only at the end (late interaction), or throughout the whole forward pass (cross-encoder).

rows: First-stage retrieval when exact terms matter

slides.title: The Bill Comes Due in Storage
bullets: Storing one vector per document token instead of one per document multiplies index size by roughly the average token count you keep embeddings for — often on the order of a hundred-plus vectors per document instead of one.

Later ColBERT work (ColBERTv2) attacks exactly this with residual compression — clustering token vectors around centroids and storing quantized offsets — shrinking the index substantially versus storing raw per-token vectors, without giving up the MaxSim mechanism.

Plain HNSW-style ANN indexes are built for single-vector nearest-neighbor search — they don't natively support 'many vectors per document, scored by MaxSim.' You need a retrieval engine or library built for multi-vector late interaction (e.g. the ColBERT/PLAID tooling, or vector databases with explicit multi-vector support).

Skip it when: your corpus is huge and storage-constrained, exact-term recall isn't your bottleneck, or a simpler bi-encoder-plus-cross-encoder-reranker pipeline already clears your quality bar — late interaction is worth its cost specifically when precision on rare terms and identifiers is what's failing today.

slides.title: Where the Interaction Happens Is the Whole Design
bullets: Bi-encoders interact never (fastest, coarsest); cross-encoders interact throughout (best quality, can't scale); late interaction interacts only at scoring time (most of the quality, most of the scalability).
MaxSim = for each query token, take its best document-token match, then sum — that's the entire scoring function, and it's cheap enough to run at query time against precomputed document matrices.
The tradeoff you're accepting is storage: many vectors per document instead of one, plus needing infrastructure that understands multi-vector scoring rather than plain nearest-neighbor search.
Reach for it when a bi-encoder is losing on exact terms — identifiers, codes, names — that a pooled vector keeps blurring away.

questions.prompt: Why can't a cross-encoder be used as the first-stage retriever over millions of documents?
options: It only outputs a single pooled vector
Its score requires both the query and document present together, so nothing about the document can be precomputed offline
It doesn't use a transformer
It can only score documents shorter than the query
questions.explanation: A cross-encoder concatenates query and document and runs full cross-attention, so the relevance score only exists once both texts are known — you'd need a fresh forward pass per query-document pair, which doesn't scale to a large corpus. That's why cross-encoders are used to rerank a small shortlist, not to search the whole index.

questions.prompt: In ColBERT's MaxSim scoring, how is the final relevance score computed?
options: Average the dot product of every query token against every document token
Take the single highest similarity across the whole document as the score
For each query token, find its highest-similarity document token, then sum those maxima across all query tokens
Concatenate the query and document token vectors and feed them through another transformer
questions.explanation: MaxSim gives each query token its own vote: it finds whichever document token it matches best, and the total score is the sum of those per-query-token maxima. That lets specific query tokens (like an exact identifier) find an exact match anywhere in the document instead of that signal being blended into one pooled vector.

questions.prompt: What's the main practical cost of late interaction retrieval compared to a standard single-vector bi-encoder?
options: It cannot be indexed offline at all
It requires a much larger index, since documents are stored as one vector per token instead of one vector total
It cannot match semantically similar words, only exact terms
It requires the query and document to be encoded by the same model call
questions.explanation: Late interaction still precomputes and indexes the document side offline — that part isn't lost. What changes is the index size: storing a vector per token (often a hundred-plus per document) instead of a single pooled vector is a real storage and infrastructure cost, which is why techniques like ColBERTv2's residual compression exist.

posts.title: GRPO: Reinforcement Learning Without a Critic
posts.subtitle: PPO needs a second neural network just to estimate a baseline — GRPO gets the same signal by making a group of answers grade each other.
posts.summary: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) replaces PPO's learned critic with a simple trick: sample a group of completions for the same prompt, score each one, and use the group's own mean and standard deviation as the baseline. That advantage estimate — no separate value network required — drops straight into a PPO-style clipped objective with a KL penalty. It's the RL algorithm behind DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1, and it works best exactly where PPO's critic struggled most: reasoning tasks with a clear, checkable reward.

slides.title: Four Models to Train One Policy? PPO Says Yes.
slides.body: Classic RLHF's PPO stage keeps four models in memory at once. GRPO throws one of them out — and gets a better baseline in the process.

slides.title: The Critic Is the Expensive, Fragile Part
bullets: PPO estimates 'how much better than expected was this action' using a learned value function (the critic) — a second network roughly the size of the policy, trained alongside it just to predict expected reward.

For LLMs the critic has to assign a value to every token position in a sequence, but the reward usually only arrives once, at the very end (e.g., 'was the final answer correct?') — that sparse signal makes the critic slow to converge and often noisy.
A bad critic doesn't just fail quietly: an inaccurate baseline produces biased advantage estimates, which push the policy in the wrong direction and destabilize training.

On top of the reward model and the frozen reference policy RLHF already needs, the critic is a fourth full-size model resident in GPU memory during training — real cost for a component whose only job is estimating a baseline.

slides.title: Let a Group of Answers Grade Each Other
bullets: For each prompt, sample a group of G completions from the current policy instead of just one — for a math problem, that means generating several independent attempts at solving it.

Score every completion in the group with the reward function (for verifiable tasks like math or code, this can just be 'did the final answer match' or 'did the tests pass' — no learned reward model required).

Compute the group's mean and standard deviation of rewards, then set each completion's advantage to (its reward − group mean) / group standard deviation — the group itself becomes the baseline, replacing the critic entirely.
That advantage plugs into the same clipped surrogate objective PPO uses, with a KL penalty against a reference policy added directly to the loss to keep updates from drifting too far in one step.

slides.title: Same Problem, Four Attempts, One Signal
bullets: Say the policy samples 4 attempts at one math problem and 2 of them land on the correct final answer: rewards = [1, 1, 0, 0].
Group mean = 0.5, group standard deviation = 0.5, so advantages work out to [+1, +1, −1, −1] — correct attempts get pushed up, incorrect ones get pushed down, in the same batch.
No critic ever ran a forward pass to produce that baseline — the group's own mean did the job.

If all 4 attempts happen to get the same reward (say all correct, or all wrong), the standard deviation is 0 and the advantage is undefined — a degenerate group that contributes no gradient signal at all.

slides.title: GRPO vs. Its Neighbors
bullets: GRPO keeps RL's core loop (sample, score, update) but removes the piece PPO needed to make that loop work — at the cost of needing many samples per prompt instead of one.

slides.title: Where GRPO Struggles
bullets: It trades critic cost for sampling cost: generating a whole group of completions per prompt at every training step means far more forward passes through the policy than PPO's single rollout.

Degenerate groups are a real failure mode — if every sampled completion in a group gets the same reward, the standard deviation collapses to zero and that batch teaches the model nothing, wasting the compute spent sampling it.

It leans on rewards that are cheap and reliable to compute at scale — GRPO shines with rule-based, verifiable rewards (correct/incorrect, tests pass/fail) and is less proven when the only reward source is a noisy learned preference model.
Larger groups give a more accurate mean/std estimate but cost proportionally more compute per update — group size is a real tuning knob, not a free lunch.

slides.title: The Group Is the Baseline
bullets: GRPO's central move: replace PPO's learned critic with the mean and standard deviation of a sampled group's rewards, then feed that advantage into the same clipped, KL-regularized update PPO already uses.

It removes an entire model from memory but adds sampling cost — a real tradeoff, not a strict improvement, and one that pays off most cleanly when rewards are cheap to verify (math, code) rather than expensive to learn.

First introduced for DeepSeekMath and later central to DeepSeek-R1's reasoning training, GRPO is now a standard option alongside PPO and DPO whenever a team has verifiable rewards and wants RL without a critic.

questions.prompt: What does GRPO use as the baseline for computing advantage, in place of PPO's learned critic?
options: A separate reward model trained on preference pairs
The mean and standard deviation of rewards across a sampled group of completions for the same prompt
A fixed constant set before training begins
The reward of the single best completion in the group
questions.explanation: GRPO samples a group of completions for each prompt, scores all of them, and normalizes each one's reward against that group's own mean and standard deviation — no learned value network needed.

questions.prompt: What happens when every completion in a GRPO sampling group receives the same reward?
options: The policy update becomes larger to compensate
The group's standard deviation is zero, so the advantage is undefined and that batch contributes no useful gradient signal
GRPO automatically falls back to using a critic for that batch
The reward model is retrained on that group
questions.explanation: Advantage in GRPO is (reward − group mean) / group standard deviation. If every sampled completion scores identically, the standard deviation collapses to zero — a degenerate group that wastes the compute spent sampling it.

questions.prompt: Compared to PPO, what does GRPO trade away in exchange for removing the critic?
options: It requires sampling multiple completions per prompt instead of just one rollout, increasing generation cost per training step
It can no longer use a KL penalty against a reference policy
It requires human preference labels for every training example
It only works with models under 10B parameters
questions.explanation: GRPO still keeps a reference policy and KL regularization — what it gives up is single-rollout efficiency. Estimating a good baseline from a group instead of a critic means generating a whole group of completions per prompt at every step.

posts.title: RoPE: Encoding Position by Rotating Query and Key Vectors
posts.subtitle: No position embedding table, no addition — just a rotation whose angle depends on where a token sits
posts.summary: Self-attention has no built-in notion of word order — shuffle the input tokens and the math doesn't change. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) fixes this not by adding a position vector to each token, but by rotating each query and key by an angle proportional to its position. The rotation's algebra makes the attention score between any two tokens depend only on their distance apart, giving relative-position awareness for free — at the cost of a hyperparameter that has to be retuned every time context length grows.

slides.title: Attention Doesn't Know What Order Words Came In
slides.body: Self-attention computes a weighted sum over all tokens using nothing but dot products between vectors — swap two tokens' positions in the input and, without help, the output is identical. Every practical transformer needs a way to inject 'where in the sequence am I' into that math. RoPE does it by rotating vectors instead of adding to them.

slides.title: Self-Attention Is Permutation-Invariant by Construction
bullets: Attention scores are dot products of query and key vectors: q·k. Nothing in that formula references token index — reorder the input sequence and, absent a position signal, attention weights reorder identically. Order is invisible to the mechanism itself.

The original 'Attention Is All You Need' transformer fixed this with sinusoidal position vectors added to each token's embedding — deterministic, no extra learned parameters, but the position signal gets mixed into the content signal from layer one.

GPT-2/BERT-style models instead learned a position embedding table (one vector per absolute position, up to some max length). This works well inside the trained range but has no principled way to handle a position it never saw during training.

Both approaches encode absolute position. What attention actually needs for most tasks is relative position — how far apart two tokens are — and neither sinusoidal addition nor a learned table makes that relationship explicit in the dot product.

slides.title: Rotate Each Query/Key Pair by an Angle Proportional to Position
bullets: RoPE (Su et al., 2021, 'RoFormer') splits each d-dimensional query/key vector into d/2 two-dimensional pairs, and rotates every pair by an angle m·θᵢ, where m is the token's position and θᵢ = base^(−2i/d) is a frequency that varies per pair.

Low-index pairs (small i) get large θᵢ and rotate quickly with position — they encode fine-grained, local position differences. High-index pairs get small θᵢ and rotate slowly — they encode coarse, long-range position differences. This mirrors the multi-frequency idea from sinusoidal encodings, but applied as a rotation, not an addition.

base is a single hyperparameter (commonly 10000 by default) that sets how fast the rotation frequencies decay across dimension pairs. It is the one knob that has to be revisited whenever a model is adapted to a longer context.

Critically, no position embedding table is learned or stored — the rotation angle is a deterministic function of position, computed on the fly and applied directly to Q and K before the attention dot product.

slides.title: Why Relative Position Falls Out of an Absolute Rotation
bullets: Rotations compose: rotating a vector by angle A and then taking its dot product with a vector rotated by angle B depends only on the angle difference (A − B), not on A and B individually — a basic property of 2D rotation matrices (R(m)ᵀR(n) = R(n−m)).

Apply that to RoPE: query at position m is rotated by mθ, key at position n is rotated by nθ. Their dot product reduces to a function of (m − n)θ alone — the absolute positions m and n cancel out, and only the relative distance survives.

So every query/key pair 'automatically' knows how far apart they are, purely as a side effect of rotation algebra — no relative-position lookup table, no extra term added to the attention score, no change to the attention formula itself.

This is the core trick: position is injected as absolute (rotate by m, rotate by n) but consumed as relative (only m − n matters), which is exactly the property useful for language, where 'three tokens back' matters far more than 'token number 47.'

slides.title: Worked Example: Same Gap, Same Score
slides.body: Take a single 2D rotation pair with frequency θ. Consider two token pairs that are 100 positions apart but sit in very different parts of a long sequence.
bullets: Pair A: query at position 5, key at position 105. After rotation, their dot product is proportional to cos(100θ) — a function of the 100-position gap only.
Pair B: query at position 1005, key at position 1105 — also 100 apart, but a thousand tokens further into the sequence. Same algebra gives the exact same cos(100θ) factor.

Absolute position (5 vs. 1005) never appears in the final score — only the gap does. This is why a RoPE-based model can, in principle, recognize 'the subject three tokens back' the same way whether that pattern occurs at token 10 or token 10,000.

The catch: this identity assumes positions stay inside the range the rotation frequencies were tuned for. Push m − n far beyond what the model saw in training and the cos(·) terms start behaving in ways the model never learned to interpret — which is exactly the long-context extrapolation problem.

slides.title: Position Encoding Schemes, Side by Side

headers: Relative position in the dot product?
rows: Yes, a full position embedding table
Encoder/decoder models with a fixed max length
Yes — falls out of rotation algebra
Yes — added directly as a distance penalty

slides.title: The Tradeoffs Nobody Puts on the Slide
bullets: Extrapolation isn't automatic: run a RoPE model on sequences much longer than it was trained on and quality degrades — the relative-position identity holds algebraically, but the model never learned to interpret rotation angles that large. Fixes like Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN rescale or reinterpret the rotation frequencies post-hoc to extend usable context.

The base hyperparameter is a real design choice, not a fixed constant: a smaller base rotates faster, giving finer local resolution but wrapping around (and losing distinguishability) sooner; a larger base slows rotation, favoring longer-range coherence at some cost to short-range precision. Models targeting much longer context typically raise it.

RoPE is inherently 1D — it encodes 'how far along the sequence.' Adapting it to 2D data like image patches (vision transformers) isn't automatic; it needs an explicit 2D/axial variant that rotates row and column position separately.

When NOT to reach for it: short, fixed-length classification models with no extrapolation requirement gain little from RoPE's relative-position machinery — a plain learned or sinusoidal embedding is simpler to reason about and just as effective inside a fixed range.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: RoPE injects position by rotating query/key vectors by an angle proportional to token position, using per-dimension-pair frequencies that range from fast (local) to slow (long-range).

Because 2D rotations compose, the attention dot product between any two rotated vectors depends only on their relative distance — relative-position awareness emerges from an absolute-position operation, with no lookup table and no extra term in the attention formula.

It's become the default in most modern decoder-only LLMs precisely because of that relative-position property and its zero-parameter footprint — but it doesn't extrapolate to unseen lengths for free, and the base hyperparameter has to be deliberately chosen or rescaled for the context length a model actually needs to serve.

Treat RoPE as 'relative position, computed cheaply' rather than 'unlimited context for free' — long-context claims still rest on how the frequencies were tuned or rescaled, not on the rotation trick alone.

questions.prompt: What problem does RoPE solve that raw self-attention has on its own?
options: Self-attention is permutation-invariant — without a position signal, reordering the input tokens doesn't change the attention output
Self-attention cannot compute dot products for vectors longer than 512 dimensions
Self-attention requires a separate softmax for every attention head
Self-attention cannot run on sequences shorter than the rotation base value
questions.explanation: Attention scores are just dot products between query and key vectors, which carry no information about token order. Some position signal has to be injected from outside the core attention formula — RoPE does it via rotation.

questions.prompt: Why does the attention score between a RoPE-rotated query and key depend only on their relative distance, not their absolute positions?
options: Because RoPE clips all position values to a fixed maximum before rotating
Because 2D rotation matrices compose so that the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference between their rotation angles
Because RoPE averages the query and key positions before computing attention
Because the base hyperparameter is set to zero for all dimension pairs
questions.explanation: Rotating a query by angle m·θ and a key by angle n·θ makes their dot product a function of (m−n)·θ — the absolute positions cancel algebraically, leaving only the relative gap, which is a basic property of rotation composition.

questions.prompt: What does RoPE's relative-position property NOT automatically give you?
options: Robust performance on sequence lengths far beyond what the model was trained on, with no further adjustment
A way to encode position without a learned embedding table
An attention score that depends on the gap between two tokens rather than their absolute indices
Zero additional learned parameters compared to a learned position embedding table
questions.explanation: The relative-position identity holds algebraically at any distance, but the model was only ever trained to interpret rotation angles up to its training context length — going far beyond it degrades quality unless techniques like Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN rescale the frequencies first.

posts.title: RLHF: Turning Human Preferences Into a Reward Signal
posts.subtitle: You can't write a demonstration for 'sounds less arrogant' — but you can rank two answers against each other.
posts.summary: RLHF trains a separate reward model on human pairwise comparisons, then uses reinforcement learning (PPO) to push the base model toward outputs that reward model scores highly — with a KL penalty keeping it tethered to the original policy so it can't drift into reward-hacking gibberish. It's expensive and unstable to run (four models in memory, a genuinely finicky RL loop), which is exactly the gap simpler alternatives like DPO were built to close.

slides.title: You Can Demonstrate an Answer. You Can't Demonstrate 'Better.'
slides.body: RLHF doesn't teach a model new facts — it teaches it which of two already-plausible answers a human would rather read.

slides.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning Has No Concept of 'Better'
bullets: SFT trains a model to imitate a fixed set of human-written demonstrations — it learns to reproduce the style and content of those examples, token by token.

But 'helpful,' 'concise,' 'not sycophantic,' and 'appropriately cautious' aren't things you can hand-write a single ground-truth demonstration for — two different answers can both be reasonable, with one just clearly preferred.

SFT alone also caps out: the model can never exceed the quality of its demonstrations, because imitation loss only ever pulls it toward what a labeler happened to type, not toward what labelers would judge as best among several options.
What's missing is a training signal built from comparisons rather than single correct answers — which is exactly what a reward model supplies.

slides.title: Three Stages: Imitate, Score, Then Optimize
bullets: Stage 1 (SFT): fine-tune the base model on human demonstrations to get a reasonable starting policy — this is the same step used with or without RLHF.

Stage 2 (reward model): show labelers several model outputs for the same prompt and have them rank which is better; train a separate model on these pairs with a Bradley-Terry loss so it learns to output a scalar score matching human preference, not just a single label.

Stage 3 (RL fine-tuning): run the SFT model as a policy, generate a response, score it with the frozen reward model, and use PPO to update the policy's weights to make higher-scoring responses more likely.
The reward model is only trained once and then frozen — it becomes the automated stand-in for a human labeler for the (much more sample-hungry) RL stage.

slides.title: Why PPO Needs a Leash
bullets: Left unconstrained, a policy chasing reward-model score will drift toward outputs the reward model rates highly but a human wouldn't — padding answers with reassurance, inflating length, repeating flattering phrases.

RLHF adds a KL-divergence penalty between the current policy and the frozen SFT model to every reward: the further the policy's output distribution strays from where it started, the more its effective reward is docked.

PPO's own clipped objective (typically clipping the policy-probability ratio to roughly a [0.8, 1.2] band) caps how much any single update can move the policy, so one batch of noisy reward signal can't swing the weights too far.
Together these two brakes are the difference between 'nudge the model toward better answers' and 'let the model discover a degenerate answer the reward model happens to love.'

slides.title: Small Model, Better Answers
bullets: OpenAI's original InstructGPT work (the RLHF recipe behind early ChatGPT) found that human labelers preferred outputs from a 1.3B-parameter RLHF-tuned model over outputs from the plain 175B-parameter GPT-3 — a 100x-smaller model, preferred more often.

Nothing about the 1.3B model's raw knowledge improved; what changed was that its outputs were shaped to match what a human labeler actually wants to read, rather than just being fluent continuations of a prompt.
This is the core case for RLHF: on tasks where 'correct' is really 'preferred,' aligning the objective to human judgment can matter more than adding parameters.

slides.title: RLHF vs. Its Simpler Alternative
bullets: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) reframes the same preference data as a classification loss with a closed-form link to the optimal RLHF policy — no reward model, no PPO rollout loop.

rows: Sensitive to reward hacking, needs careful tuning

slides.title: Where It Breaks: Reward Hacking and Cost
bullets: Reward hacking (Goodhart's law in practice): once the policy starts optimizing against a learned proxy instead of real human judgment, it finds the proxy's blind spots — well-documented failure modes include length bias (longer answers scoring higher regardless of quality) and sycophancy (agreeing with the user to score well).

Running the pipeline is expensive: the RL stage needs the policy, a frozen reference copy, the reward model, and (for PPO) a value model all resident at once, plus the reward model's own labeled-comparison dataset to train in the first place.
PPO is a genuinely finicky optimizer for this setting — reward variance, KL-coefficient tuning, and batch-size choices all meaningfully affect whether training converges cleanly or degenerates.

There's also an 'alignment tax': models tuned hard against a preference reward sometimes regress slightly on raw capability benchmarks relative to the SFT checkpoint they started from, trading some sharpness for likability.

slides.title: A Comparison Signal, Carefully Leashed
bullets: RLHF's core idea: train a reward model on human comparisons, then use RL to optimize the policy against that learned reward instead of against fixed demonstrations.
The KL penalty against a frozen reference policy is what keeps optimization honest — remove it and the policy will find whatever the reward model misjudges.

It's costly and unstable enough that DPO (a single supervised loss over the same preference pairs) has become the default choice when the goal is simplicity; RLHF still shows up where the extra RL flexibility (e.g. optimizing non-differentiable or multi-objective rewards) is worth the overhead.

questions.prompt: What does the reward model in RLHF actually learn to do?
options: Predict the next token in a sequence
Output a scalar score that matches which of two candidate responses a human labeler preferred
Generate new training demonstrations automatically
Translate text between languages for multilingual training data
questions.explanation: The reward model is trained on human pairwise comparisons using a Bradley-Terry-style loss, so it learns to assign higher scores to responses humans ranked as better. It then stands in for a human labeler during the much more sample-hungry RL stage.

questions.prompt: Why does RLHF add a KL-divergence penalty against a frozen reference policy during PPO?
options: To make the reward model smaller and cheaper to run
To speed up convergence by increasing the learning rate
To stop the policy from drifting so far from its starting point that it exploits blind spots in the reward model (reward hacking)
To remove the need for human comparison data entirely
questions.explanation: Without a leash, a policy that only chases reward-model score can find degenerate outputs the reward model over-rates — like padding length or excessive agreement. The KL penalty docks reward as the policy strays from the reference, keeping updates tethered to reasonable behavior.

questions.prompt: How does DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) differ from classic RLHF?
options: DPO requires a larger reward model than RLHF
DPO trains directly on a supervised classification loss over preference pairs, skipping the separate reward model and PPO rollout loop
DPO doesn't use any human preference data
DPO can only be applied after RLHF has already been run
questions.explanation: DPO uses the same kind of pairwise preference data as RLHF, but exploits a closed-form relationship between reward and optimal policy to turn the whole problem into a single supervised loss — no reward model to train, no reinforcement learning loop to stabilize.

posts.title: Constrained Decoding: Making Invalid Output Impossible
posts.subtitle: Instead of hoping the model emits valid JSON, make invalid tokens unsampleable.
posts.summary: Constrained decoding masks an LLM's logits at every step so only tokens legal under a grammar (a JSON Schema, a regex, a CFG) can be sampled, making malformed output structurally impossible instead of merely unlikely. It guarantees syntax, not truth — and forcing structure too early can blunt a model's reasoning, so the sharpest use pairs free-form thinking with a constrained final step.

slides.title: Stop Hoping the JSON Parses
slides.body: Constrained decoding doesn't ask the model to follow a format — it removes every token that would break it from the sampling pool.

slides.title: Prompting for Format Is a Request, Not a Guarantee
bullets: Ask a model to 'respond with only valid JSON matching this schema' and it usually complies — until a trailing comma, an unescaped quote, a wrong type, or an extra field on maybe 1 in 50 calls breaks the parser.
The standard fix is retry-on-failure: parse, catch the exception, resend the same prompt with the error appended. That burns tokens, adds latency, and still has no upper bound on attempts.
For an agent chaining ten tool calls, a 2% per-call failure rate compounds into an ~18% chance at least one call in the chain needs a retry — enough to make pipelines flaky in production.

slides.title: Compile the Schema Into a Grammar, Mask the Logits
bullets: A JSON Schema, regex, or context-free grammar is compiled into a state machine: at any point in the output, the automaton knows exactly which next characters are legal.

Before sampling each token, the decoder maps the automaton's currently-legal continuations onto the model's vocabulary and sets the logits of every other token to -infinity — the model literally cannot pick them.
The model still chooses freely among whatever remains legal, so it's picking the 'best' valid token at each step rather than being told a fixed string — output stays diverse within the allowed shape.

slides.title: The Hard Part Is Token Boundaries, Not Grammars
bullets: LLMs sample subword tokens, not characters, so a naive implementation would need to check every one of ~100k vocabulary entries against the grammar at every step — too slow to be usable.

Production libraries (Outlines, llama.cpp's GBNF, xgrammar, and the engines behind OpenAI's and Anthropic's structured-output APIs) precompute which tokens are ever reachable from each automaton state, so masking is a fast lookup instead of a live simulation.

A token can also straddle a boundary the grammar cares about (e.g. a BPE piece like ' "}' closes a string and the object in one token) — the automaton has to be advanced per-token, not per-character, or the mask silently drifts out of sync.

slides.title: A Weather Tool Call, Constrained
bullets: Schema: {"city": string, "days": integer 1-10}. Unconstrained, a model might emit {"city": "Boston", "days": "5"} — a string where an integer was required, which a strict tool-calling layer rejects.
With the schema compiled to a grammar, the decoder won't let the model open a quote after `"days": ` at all — only digit tokens are legal there, so a string-typed value can never be sampled.
The same mechanism enforces days staying within 1-10 if the grammar encodes the range, catching a structurally-valid-but-out-of-bounds value before it ever reaches the tool.

slides.title: Three Ways to Get Structured Output
bullets: Constrained decoding is the only approach where 'invalid syntax' becomes impossible rather than merely penalized or caught after the fact.

slides.title: Guaranteed Syntax Isn't Guaranteed Sense — and Timing Matters
bullets: Constrained decoding proves the output is well-formed, never that it's correct: a schema-valid {"city": "Atlantis", "days": 5} is exactly as syntactically legal as a real one.

Forcing structure from the very first token also removes the model's room to reason — chain-of-thought text can't appear inside a field the grammar has locked down, which measurably hurts accuracy on tasks that benefit from working through the problem first.
The common fix: let the model think in free, unconstrained text first, then apply the grammar only to a final short 'extraction' step that turns the reasoning into the structured answer.

Skip it for loosely-shaped or creative output where 'valid shape' isn't the risk — the overhead of building and maintaining a grammar isn't worth it when a malformed response is rare and cheap to catch downstream anyway.

slides.title: Move the Guarantee Into the Sampler
bullets: Constrained decoding turns 'please output valid JSON' from a request into a structural fact by masking illegal tokens out of the sampling distribution at every step.
It's a syntax guarantee, not a truth guarantee — pair it with validation logic for anything that actually needs to be correct, not just well-formed.
Reach for it on tool calls and API-facing outputs where a parser is waiting on the other end; let reasoning-heavy answers run unconstrained until the final structured step.

questions.prompt: How does constrained decoding stop an LLM from producing malformed JSON?
options: It fine-tunes the model on JSON examples before inference
It masks the logits of any token that would violate the compiled grammar, so illegal tokens can't be sampled
It asks a second model to reformat the output afterward
It lowers the temperature to zero
questions.explanation: The grammar (from a JSON Schema, regex, or CFG) is compiled into a state machine that tracks which tokens are legal at each step; the decoder sets every illegal token's logit to -infinity before sampling, so the model is structurally incapable of picking them.

questions.prompt: What does constrained decoding NOT guarantee?
options: That the output matches the schema's structure
That every required field is present
That the field values are factually or semantically correct
That types (string vs integer) match the schema
questions.explanation: It guarantees syntactic validity by construction, but a schema-valid value can still be wrong or made up — {"city": "Atlantis"} is just as well-formed as a real city. Semantic correctness needs separate validation.

questions.prompt: Why can forcing a grammar from the very first output token hurt accuracy on reasoning-heavy tasks?
options: Grammars are always slower than free-form generation
It removes room for chain-of-thought text, since reasoning can't appear inside a field the grammar has already locked down
It forces the model to use a smaller vocabulary permanently
It disables sampling entirely
questions.explanation: If the schema is applied from token one, there's nowhere for the model to think out loud before answering. The common fix is to let it reason in unconstrained text first, then apply the grammar only to a short final extraction step.

posts.title: MCP Roots: A Boundary the Server Isn't Forced to Respect
posts.subtitle: The third MCP primitive — and the one everyone assumes is a sandbox.
posts.summary: MCP roots let a client tell a server which directories matter for the current session — a list of {uri, name} pairs kept current via list_changed notifications. It's the third primitive alongside Sampling and Elicitation, and the spec is explicit that it's a scoping hint, not an enforced security boundary.

slides.title: A Client Draws the Map, a Server Reads It
slides.body: MCP roots let a client tell a server which directories are relevant to the current session — a scoping hint, not a security wall.

slides.title: A Filesystem Server Given the Whole Disk
bullets: Point a generic filesystem MCP server at a machine and it has no idea whether the user's actual workspace is one repo, three open projects, or a single config file — everything is technically reachable.
Before roots, a server either hardcoded a path, made the developer configure one per deployment, or exposed tools broad enough to touch anything the process account could see.

slides.title: The Client Advertises roots, the Server Calls roots/list
bullets: At initialization, a client that supports the feature declares a `roots` capability; a server that cares can then send a `roots/list` request.
The client responds with an array of roots, each a `{ uri, name }` pair — uri is almost always a `file://` URI, name is a human-readable label like 'project-a'.
The server treats the returned URIs as its working set: it scopes tool descriptions, resource listings, and default search paths to stay inside them.

slides.title: Roots Change — list_changed Keeps the Server Current
bullets: A user opening or closing a workspace folder mid-session changes what's actually relevant — MCP doesn't require the server to poll to catch that.
The client sends `notifications/roots/list_changed` whenever the set changes; a well-behaved server re-issues `roots/list` and updates its own scoping instead of working from a stale snapshot.
This is push-based and asynchronous — the server doesn't block waiting on it, it just knows a refresh is available.

slides.title: Two Projects Open, One Folder Deliberately Excluded
bullets: A developer has `~/project-a` and `~/project-b` open in their editor, plus an unrelated `~/secrets` folder elsewhere on disk that was never added to the workspace.

The client's roots list contains only project-a and project-b. A filesystem MCP server built to respect roots scopes its `list_files` and `read_file` tools — and the model's own tool-call suggestions — to those two trees.
Nothing in the protocol stops the server process from opening a path under `~/secrets` anyway — it simply was never told that folder was in scope, so a cooperative server has no reason to look there.

slides.title: Roots vs. the Other MCP Primitives
bullets: Roots is the only primitive that flows client -> server as pure scope, with no model or human directly in the loop.

rows: Client tells server which directories are in scope
Server borrows the client's LLM to reason
Server asks the human a direct question mid-call

slides.title: Advisory, Not a Sandbox — Don't Confuse the Two
bullets: The spec is explicit that roots are informational: nothing in MCP mechanically prevents a server from requesting a path outside the declared roots, and nothing forces the client to reject such a request either.
Real access control has to come from somewhere else — OS file permissions, a sandboxed process, or the server implementation choosing to validate paths against the roots it was given.

Skip roots for single-purpose servers with an already-narrow, fixed scope — a server that only ever touches one config file gains nothing from asking. Reach for it when a general-purpose tool needs to infer 'relevant' from a workspace that changes session to session.

slides.title: A Scoping Hint, Not a Permission System
bullets: Roots exist so a general-purpose server can infer what 'the project' means without hardcoding a path or being configured once at deploy time.
list_changed keeps that scope current as the user opens and closes workspace folders, without the server polling for it.
Treat it as intent, not enforcement — pair roots with real sandboxing or path validation on the server side if the data actually needs protecting.

questions.prompt: What does an MCP client send when a server calls roots/list?
options: An OAuth access token
An array of {uri, name} pairs describing relevant directories
The full contents of every open file
A JSON Schema for form input
questions.explanation: roots/list returns a list of URI/name pairs — almost always file:// paths — describing which directories are currently relevant to the session, not file contents or credentials.

questions.prompt: What triggers a notifications/roots/list_changed message?
options: Every tool call the server makes
The set of relevant directories changing, e.g. the user opening or closing a workspace folder
The server requesting more permissions
A scheduled polling interval
questions.explanation: list_changed is push-based: the client sends it whenever the actual set of roots changes, so the server can refresh instead of polling or working from a stale list.

questions.prompt: Why can't roots be relied on as a security boundary by themselves?
options: Because they use JSON Schema, which is inherently insecure
Because nothing in the protocol stops a server from requesting or accessing paths outside the declared roots
Because roots require OAuth to function
Because only Advanced-difficulty servers support them
questions.explanation: Roots are advisory — they communicate scope, not enforce it. Real protection still needs OS permissions, sandboxing, or server-side path validation on top.

posts.title: A2A Protocol: When One Agent Delegates to Another
posts.subtitle: MCP connects an agent to tools. A2A connects one agent to a completely different one.
posts.summary: Agent2Agent (A2A) is Google's open protocol for letting independent AI agents — built by different teams, on different frameworks — discover each other, negotiate a task, and exchange results without either side seeing the other's internals. It solves a different problem than MCP: MCP wires one agent to tools and data; A2A wires one agent to another agent treated as a peer.

slides.title: Your Agent Needs to Delegate to Someone Else's Agent
slides.body: An orchestrator agent needs a hotel search done. The best hotel-search agent for the job was built by a different company, on a different framework, and exposes none of its internal code. MCP doesn't solve this — it wires an agent to tools and data it already trusts, not to another autonomous agent it's never met.

slides.title: MCP Standardizes Tools. It Doesn't Standardize Agents Talking to Agents.
bullets: MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives one agent a standard way to call tools and pull context from data sources it already trusts — the tool's internals are irrelevant, only its schema matters.
That model breaks down when the 'tool' is itself an autonomous agent: it might take minutes or hours, ask a clarifying question mid-task, stream partial progress, or need to be told to stop.

Before A2A, every vendor wanting cross-agent collaboration had to build a custom, incompatible integration — an orchestrator from one framework couldn't hand work to a specialist agent built on another.
Google announced Agent2Agent (A2A) in April 2025 as an open protocol for exactly this: independent, opaque agents discovering each other and delegating work as peers, not as tool-and-caller.

slides.title: Agent Cards, Tasks, and Artifacts
bullets: Agent Card: a JSON manifest a server publishes describing what it can do, how to reach it, and what auth it requires — the client fetches this first, the same way a browser fetches a manifest before rendering a page.
Task: the unit of work. A client sends a task, the remote agent works it through a lifecycle — submitted, working, possibly input-required if it needs a clarifying answer, then completed or failed.
Message and Artifact: messages are the turns of the exchange (text, files, structured data); artifacts are what the remote agent hands back when it's done — the actual deliverable, not just a status.
Long-running tasks stream incremental updates rather than forcing the client to poll blindly, so an hours-long research task and a one-second lookup use the same protocol shape.

slides.title: A2A vs. MCP: Different Layers of the Same Stack

rows: An agent to tools and data sources
An agent to another independent agent
A tool call (schema in, result out)
A task with a lifecycle (can span minutes to hours)
Tool/resource schema exposed by the server
Agent Card published by the remote agent
Caller trusts and inspects the tool
Peers stay opaque — internals aren't shared
Give one agent a database, a file system, an API
Have one agent's orchestrator delegate to a specialist agent

slides.title: Worked Example: A Travel Orchestrator Delegates to a Hotel Specialist
slides.body: An orchestrator agent is planning a trip. Hotel search isn't its specialty — a separate vendor runs a hotel-search agent that's genuinely better at it.
bullets: 1. Discovery: the orchestrator fetches the hotel agent's Agent Card, sees it accepts a destination, date range, and budget, and supports streaming updates.

2. Delegation: it sends a Task with those parameters as a Message. The hotel agent doesn't get the orchestrator's other context — trip budget logic, the user's full itinerary — only what was explicitly passed.
3. Mid-task: the hotel agent flags the task input-required because the date range spans a local holiday with sparse inventory; it asks whether to widen the search window.
4. Completion: once resolved, the task moves to completed and returns an Artifact — a structured list of hotel options — which the orchestrator folds back into the itinerary it's building.

slides.title: When A2A Is Overkill — and Its Real Adoption Signal
bullets: Don't reach for A2A to call your own in-process function or a tool you fully control — that's exactly what MCP (or a plain function call) already does more simply.

A2A adds real overhead: publishing and maintaining an Agent Card, handling a task lifecycle, thinking about auth for a party you don't control — worth it only when the other side is genuinely a separate, opaque agent.
Publishing an Agent Card is also a trust surface: anyone who can reach it can attempt to invoke your agent, so authentication and rate-limiting on the endpoint matter from day one.

The protocol isn't just a Google side-project: it was contributed to the Linux Foundation in June 2025 for vendor-neutral governance, and adopters cited by Google include Adobe, ServiceNow, and Twilio building cross-vendor agent workflows on it.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: A2A and MCP solve different layers: MCP is agent-to-tool (bring context and capabilities into one agent); A2A is agent-to-agent (let two independent agents discover each other and delegate work as peers).
The core objects are an Agent Card (what a remote agent can do and how to reach it), a Task (a unit of work with a lifecycle, not just a single call), and Artifacts (the actual output handed back).
Peers stay opaque on purpose — a delegating agent doesn't see the other side's reasoning or internals, only its declared capabilities and its output.
Use it when you're genuinely crossing an organizational or framework boundary between two autonomous agents; for tools and data you already control, MCP (or a direct call) is simpler and sufficient.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between what MCP standardizes and what A2A standardizes?
options: MCP is for text-only agents, A2A is for multimodal agents
MCP connects an agent to tools and data it already trusts; A2A connects one agent to a separate, independent agent treated as a peer
They are two names for the exact same protocol
MCP is Google's protocol and A2A is Anthropic's protocol
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes agent-to-tool/data connections where the caller trusts and inspects the tool's schema. A2A standardizes agent-to-agent delegation, where both sides stay opaque to each other and interact only through declared capabilities and task results.

questions.prompt: In A2A, what does a client fetch first before delegating work to a remote agent?
options: The remote agent's full source code
A live video demo of the agent
The Agent Card — a JSON manifest describing capabilities, endpoint, and required auth
A signed contract from the agent's vendor
questions.explanation: The Agent Card is the discovery mechanism: a published manifest describing what the remote agent can do and how to reach it, fetched before any task is sent — analogous to a service's public API description.

questions.prompt: Why might an A2A Task move into an 'input-required' state instead of straight to 'completed'?
options: The protocol requires every task to pause once at random
The remote agent needs a clarifying answer mid-task before it can finish — for example, an ambiguous date range — so the lifecycle pauses for that input
It means the task has permanently failed
It only happens when the network connection drops
questions.explanation: A2A models tasks as a lifecycle, not a single blocking call, specifically so a long-running or ambiguous task can pause for clarification (input-required) rather than failing outright or guessing.
