posts.title: Attention Sinks: Why the First Few Tokens Never Get Evicted
posts.subtitle: Evict the start of the sequence from a streaming KV cache and perplexity explodes — here's why
posts.summary: A handful of early tokens in any sequence absorb a wildly disproportionate share of attention across heads and layers, almost independent of what they actually say. Evict them from a streaming KV cache, as a naive sliding window does, and every later token's attention destabilizes — but keep just four of them pinned in place alongside a normal rolling window, and an already-trained model can stream generation indefinitely with constant memory and stable quality.

slides.title: Evict the Oldest Tokens and Perplexity Explodes
slides.body: Bound a streaming LLM's memory with the obvious fix — a sliding window that drops the oldest tokens as new ones arrive — and generation quality doesn't just drift, it collapses. The cause isn't lost content. It's a handful of early tokens the model has learned to lean on for something else entirely.

slides.title: A Sliding Window Alone Breaks Down the Moment It Starts Evicting
bullets: To keep a KV cache bounded during long or open-ended generation, the obvious fix is a sliding window: keep only the most recent K tokens, dropping the oldest one each time a new one arrives.

Empirically, the moment eviction starts — the window no longer contains token 0 — perplexity spikes sharply, even though the window still holds a perfectly coherent, locally-relevant stretch of recent text.

The cause isn't that the model 'forgets' distant content. Researchers found the first few tokens of any sequence receive a disproportionately large share of attention across nearly every head and layer, almost regardless of their semantic content.

Remove those tokens and every later token's softmax loses a landing zone it has learned to dump excess attention mass into — attention distributions elsewhere become unstable, and output quality craters.

slides.title: Pin a Few Early Tokens, Let the Rest Slide
bullets: This is the 'attention sink' phenomenon (StreamingLLM, 2023): a small number of early tokens act as a dumping ground for attention mass, largely independent of their actual content.

The fix is to never evict them. Keep a tiny fixed set of 'sink' tokens — the original study found just 4 was already enough — permanently resident in the KV cache, alongside a normal sliding window of recent tokens.
The cache becomes two regions: a fixed short prefix of sink tokens, plus a rolling window of the most recent tokens. Total cache size stays bounded no matter how long generation runs.

Crucially, this works on models that were never trained with sinks in mind — they already learned to rely on early-token sinks during ordinary pretraining, so the fix requires no retraining or fine-tuning.

slides.title: Two Regions, One Cache, Bounded Memory Forever
bullets: Layout: [sink tokens, fixed] + [window tokens, rolling]. When a new token arrives and the window is full, only the oldest window token is evicted — the sink region is never touched.

Position ids are reassigned relative to the current contents of the cache, not the token's true position in the original sequence — so rotary/relative position encodings stay valid no matter how many tokens have streamed past.

The sink tokens don't need to be special or content-rich — even the first few ordinary tokens of the prompt work, because the effect is structural (a side effect of how softmax normalizes attention), not semantic.
Because cache size is now (sink count + window size) instead of (total tokens seen), memory and per-step compute stay flat indefinitely — the same cost at token 1,000 as at token 1,000,000.

slides.title: Worked Example: A Support Bot That Never Restarts
slides.body: A chat assistant runs for days across thousands of turns, streaming tokens continuously rather than restarting its context each session.
bullets: Plain sliding window (window = 2048, no sinks): once total tokens pass ~2048 and the first tokens get evicted, perplexity spikes almost immediately — replies visibly degrade into repetition, broken formatting, and incoherent references.

Attention sinks (4 pinned tokens + window = 2048): cache size stays essentially the same (~2052 tokens), but perplexity stays flat and stable through the entire run, reported in the original study as stable even after streaming millions of tokens.

What it does not do: the bot can't recall the literal content of turn 1 by turn 10,000 — the sink tokens stabilize attention, they don't store conversation history. Real long-term recall still needs a separate memory or retrieval layer on top.

slides.title: Dense Attention vs. Plain Window vs. Attention Sinks

headers: Behavior once the window limit is passed
rows: Stable quality, but memory eventually blows up
Perplexity spikes sharply the moment eviction begins
Perplexity stays stable, reported comparable to dense attention over very long streams

slides.title: What Attention Sinks Don't Fix
bullets: They stabilize attention math, not memory: content evicted from the sliding window is genuinely gone from the cache — the model cannot recall specific facts from outside its window just because sinks are present.

They're not a substitute for real long-context capability. Tasks that need actual long-document recall still want extended-context training or retrieval-augmented approaches, not just a streaming trick.

More sinks isn't obviously better: the original study found ~4 already sufficient, while zero sinks (a plain window) collapses quality — over-allocating sink tokens mostly just spends cache budget for no extra benefit.

Remapped positions mean the model's internal notion of 'how far back' a token is no longer matches its true position in the original conversation — fine for streaming coherence, but worth knowing if downstream logic is position-sensitive.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: The 'attention sink' phenomenon: a handful of early tokens absorb disproportionate attention mass across heads and layers, mostly independent of their content — an emergent side effect of softmax attention, not something those tokens semantically 'deserve.'

Naively evicting them (a plain sliding window) destabilizes attention everywhere else and craters quality; pinning just a few of them (commonly 4) alongside a normal rolling window fixes it with zero retraining.
This is what lets an already-trained LLM stream open-ended generation with constant, bounded memory instead of a KV cache that grows forever.
It buys stability and bounded memory, not extended recall — pair it with real long-context training or retrieval when the task actually needs the model to remember far-back content.

questions.prompt: What is the 'attention sink' phenomenon?
options: The first few tokens in a sequence absorb a disproportionate share of attention across most heads and layers, largely independent of their content
The KV cache physically overflows once it exceeds GPU memory
Attention scores between adjacent tokens are always the highest in the sequence
A kernel-level bug that causes some tokens to be silently dropped
questions.explanation: It's an emergent property of how softmax attention distributes probability mass, not something tied to what those early tokens actually mean — models consistently over-attend to the first few positions regardless of content.

questions.prompt: Why does a plain sliding window (no sink tokens) cause perplexity to spike once eviction begins?
options: The window becomes too large to fit in GPU memory
Evicting the early tokens removes a landing zone that later tokens' attention distributions have learned to rely on, destabilizing attention throughout the sequence
The model runs out of valid position ids once the window slides
The remaining tokens in the window stop being semantically related to each other
questions.explanation: The instability isn't about losing meaningful content — it's structural. Once the sink tokens are gone, every other token's attention distribution, which was implicitly counting on that landing zone, becomes unstable.

questions.prompt: What does adding attention sinks NOT give you?
options: Bounded, constant memory during long streaming generation
Stability that avoids retraining an already-trained model
Genuine recall of specific content that was evicted from the sliding window
Perplexity comparable to dense (unbounded) attention over long streams
questions.explanation: Sinks stabilize the attention math — they don't store or retrieve content that fell out of the window. Actual long-range recall is a separate problem, solved by long-context training or retrieval, not by attention sinks.

posts.title: Continuous Batching: Stop Waiting for the Slowest Request
posts.subtitle: Why LLM servers reschedule the batch every single token, not every request
posts.summary: Batching multiple requests together is how LLM servers keep GPUs busy, but batching at the request level forces short answers to wait for the longest one in the batch to finish. Continuous batching reschedules the running batch after every decoded token instead of every full request, evicting finished sequences and admitting new ones mid-flight so GPU slots almost never sit idle.

slides.title: A Finished Reply Still Held Its GPU Slot Hostage
slides.body: Naive batching treats a batch of requests as one atomic unit: if one reply needs 500 tokens and the rest need 20, everyone waits for the 500-token reply — the GPU keeps computing on slots that are done in every way that matters, just not officially closed.

slides.title: Request-Level Batching Waits for the Slowest Sequence
bullets: Classic batching groups N requests into one fixed batch and runs the model forward, one decoding step at a time, until every sequence in that batch hits its stop token or max length
A sequence that finishes early can't leave — its slot either sits idle or gets padded, but a new waiting request can't take that slot until the whole batch drains
The result is a convoy effect: one long-running request (a big summarization, a long chain-of-thought answer) drags down throughput for every short request unlucky enough to share its batch
Queued requests outside the batch keep waiting even though the GPU has computationally free slots right now — the batch boundary is what's blocking them, not the hardware

slides.title: Reschedule at the Token Level, Not the Batch Level
bullets: Continuous batching (also called iteration-level scheduling or in-flight batching) runs the scheduler after every single decoding step — every generated token — instead of after the whole batch finishes
The moment a sequence emits its stop token or hits max length, it's evicted immediately, freeing its slot for the very next iteration
A waiting request in the queue gets inserted into that freed slot right away — it doesn't wait for anyone else in the batch to finish, only for the next forward pass
Batch composition is fluid: the set of sequences being computed together can be completely different from one iteration to the next

slides.title: It Needs a Memory Manager That Can Keep Up
bullets: Sequences entering and leaving the batch every iteration means the KV cache can't live in one fixed-size contiguous tensor sized for a static batch — allocations and frees happen constantly, at unpredictable moments
This is why continuous batching is almost always paired with a per-sequence, block-based KV cache allocator (the same idea behind paged attention) rather than one big preallocated buffer

New requests bring a prompt that must be 'prefilled' — processed all at once, which is compute-heavy — while ongoing sequences are in 'decode', generating one token at a time, which is memory-bandwidth-heavy

Mixing a large prefill into the same iteration as many decode steps spikes that iteration's latency for every decode sequence sharing it, which is why production schedulers often chunk large prefills across several iterations instead of running them in one shot

slides.title: Worked Example: Four Requests, Wildly Different Lengths
slides.body: Say four requests join a batch needing 20, 20, 200, and 20 output tokens respectively.
bullets: Static batching: the server runs all 200 steps for all four slots. Three slots finish real work at step 20 and then just occupy GPU memory — doing nothing useful — for the remaining 180 steps. Any request that arrived at step 21 waits until step 200

Continuous batching: at step 20, the three short sequences are evicted the instant they finish. If three new requests are waiting, they take those slots at step 21 — they don't wait 180 extra steps for an unrelated request to finish
The long 200-token request is unaffected either way — continuous batching doesn't speed up any single sequence, it stops other sequences from being blocked by it

slides.title: Static Batching vs. Continuous Batching

rows: Once per full batch (waits for the slowest sequence)
Once per decoding iteration (per generated token)
Drops as short sequences finish but can't leave
Stays high — freed slots refill on the next step
Until the current batch fully drains
Until the next iteration, regardless of batch state
One fixed-size buffer sized for the batch

slides.title: Where It Gets Hard — and Where It Doesn't Help
bullets: It adds real scheduler complexity: per-iteration admission decisions, prefill/decode interleaving, and eviction all have to happen every single step without becoming the bottleneck themselves
Admitting too many concurrent sequences too eagerly can exhaust KV cache memory — the scheduler has to reserve headroom or evict/preempt lower-priority sequences under pressure
It doesn't shrink the work for any individual request — a 500-token reply still takes roughly 500 steps to generate; continuous batching only prevents that request from stalling everyone else

For a server that only ever handles one request at a time, or where all requests are near-identical length (e.g. fixed-length classification-style outputs), the benefit shrinks — there's little convoy effect to fix

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Naive batching is atomic at the request level — one long sequence in a batch drags every other slot down with it until the whole batch finishes
Continuous batching reschedules at the granularity of a single decoding step, evicting finished sequences and admitting queued ones on the very next iteration
It typically requires a per-sequence, block-based KV cache manager, since batch membership changes unpredictably every step rather than at fixed boundaries
It's a throughput and utilization fix, not a latency fix for any one request — mixing prefill and decode work still needs care, usually via chunked prefill

questions.prompt: Under naive request-level batching, what specifically causes GPU slots to sit idle?
options: The model weights don't fit in GPU memory
A slot freed by an early-finishing sequence can't be reused until every sequence in that same batch also finishes
The scheduler prioritizes requests by billing tier
Attention computation scales quadratically with sequence length
questions.explanation: Request-level batching treats the whole batch as one atomic unit. A short sequence that finishes early has nowhere to go — its slot stays occupied (idle or padded) until the batch's longest sequence also finishes, since new requests can only join at a batch boundary.

questions.prompt: At what granularity does continuous batching re-evaluate which sequences are running?
options: Once per request, at admission time only
Once per full batch, after every sequence completes
Every single decoding iteration — one generated token per active sequence
On a fixed timer, independent of generation progress
questions.explanation: Continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling) checks batch membership after every forward pass. A sequence that just finished is evicted immediately, and a queued request can take its slot on the very next step.

questions.prompt: Why is admitting a new request's full prompt (prefill) into a busy decode-heavy iteration risky?
options: Prefill requires different model weights than decode
Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is compute-heavy, which can spike that iteration's latency for every decode-phase sequence sharing the step
Prefill can only run on CPU, not GPU
Decode-phase sequences must be fully paused and restarted afterward
questions.explanation: Prefill and decode have very different compute profiles — prefill is compute-bound (processing many prompt tokens at once), decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (one token at a time). Mixing a large prefill into a decode-heavy step slows down every sequence in that step, which is why servers often chunk large prefills across several iterations instead.

posts.title: SWE-Bench ProMax: Refactoring Breaks Coding Agents
posts.subtitle: 170 real multilingual refactors, and the best agent still fails 6 in 10
posts.summary: SWE-Bench ProMax is a new 170-instance, seven-language refactoring benchmark built because SWE-bench Verified was showing cracks — nearly 60% of its unsolved instances turned out to have flawed tests. Under two agent scaffolds, the best frontier model resolved only 41.2% of ProMax's tasks, showing refactoring is a harder, less contaminated test of coding agents than bug-fixing.

slides.title: The Benchmark Coding Agents Were Acing Had a Crack in It
slides.body: SWE-bench Verified became the industry's go-to yardstick for coding agents. A new audit found nearly 60% of its still-unsolved instances have broken tests — and researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and HKUST built a harder, cleaner replacement out of real-world refactors.

slides.title: Old Benchmarks Were Saturating and Leaking
bullets: An audit of SWE-bench Verified found close to 60% of its unsolved instances have flawed tests — either too narrow (rejecting genuinely correct fixes) or too broad (silently demanding unstated behavior)
Frontier models can reproduce gold patches near-verbatim on some instances, a sign of training-data contamination rather than genuine problem-solving
Most prior benchmarks are single-file, Python-only bug fixes — a narrow slice of what real engineering work looks like
As leaderboard scores climbed past 70-80%, it got hard to tell whether agents were actually improving or the benchmark was just leaking answers

slides.title: 170 Real Refactors Across Seven Languages
bullets: SWE-Bench ProMax draws 170 expert-curated instances from real commits across Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, and Rust
Every task is a refactor — a behavior-preserving change spanning multiple files — not a single localized bug fix
Authored by a 15-person team led by Yuling Shi (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) with Shing-Chi Cheung (HKUST) and collaborators, published on arXiv this week
Agents are evaluated under two different agent scaffolds, so the score reflects the task's difficulty rather than one harness's quirks

slides.title: Worked Example: Renaming an API Across a Codebase
slides.body: A typical ProMax instance: rename a widely-used function signature in a Go service, then update every call site, every mock, and every test that depends on the old shape — without changing observable behavior anywhere.
bullets: A single-file bug fix lets an agent patch one function and move on; this task requires tracking every downstream consumer across the repo
Miss one call site and the build breaks; over-edit an unrelated function and you've silently changed behavior the tests never checked for
There's no single 'diff' that obviously encodes the fix the way a bug-fix patch does — the agent has to hold the whole change's intent in mind across many edits

slides.title: How ProMax Differs From SWE-bench Verified

rows: Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, Rust
~60% of unsolved instances have flawed tests
Newly built, expert-curated to avoid the same trap

slides.title: Why Refactoring Is a Harder Mechanism to Get Right
bullets: Bug fixes are usually local: find the broken line, change it, done. Refactors are global: an edit in one file implies required edits in N others
The agent must maintain a consistent invariant (the old and new versions must behave identically) across every touched file, not just make tests pass
Grading is harder too — a passing test suite doesn't prove behavior preservation if the suite doesn't cover every changed path, which is exactly the gap ProMax's expert curation targets

slides.title: What ProMax Doesn't Solve
bullets: 170 instances is small next to SWE-bench's thousands — enough for a stress test, not yet a broad leaderboard
It's brand new (posted this week), so there's no independent, cross-lab leaderboard yet to confirm the 41.2% figure holds up under different harnesses
Only two agent scaffolds were tested; a differently engineered agent harness could plausibly score higher or lower on the same models

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: SWE-bench Verified was showing saturation and contamination signs — nearly 60% of its unsolved instances have flawed tests
SWE-Bench ProMax replaces single-file bug fixes with multi-file, behavior-preserving refactors across seven languages
Even the best frontier model under the best of two scaffolds resolved only 41.2% of tasks — refactoring is unsaturated and genuinely hard
Expect refactoring-style benchmarks to matter more as bug-fixing benchmarks get contaminated or memorized

questions.prompt: What resolve rate did the best-performing model achieve on SWE-Bench ProMax?
questions.explanation: Under the best of two agent scaffolds, the top model resolved only 41.2% of ProMax's 170 refactoring tasks — showing the benchmark is far from saturated.

questions.prompt: What problem with SWE-bench Verified motivated building ProMax?
options: It only supports closed-source models
An audit found nearly 60% of its unsolved instances have flawed tests, and some gold patches can be reproduced near-verbatim from training data
It has no public leaderboard
It only tests documentation generation
questions.explanation: The flawed-test finding (tests too narrow or too broad) plus signs of verbatim patch reproduction meant high scores on Verified didn't reliably mean genuine problem-solving anymore.

questions.prompt: Why is a multi-file refactor mechanically harder for an agent than a single-file bug fix?
options: Refactors always require more tokens of output
The agent must keep a consistent behavior-preserving invariant across every file it touches, not just make one local edit pass a test
Refactors don't involve any test suite at all
Refactors are always shorter, so agents get less context to work with
questions.explanation: A bug fix is usually local — find and change one broken spot. A refactor implies coordinated edits across many files that must all stay behaviorally consistent, which is much easier to get subtly wrong.

posts.title: FlashAttention: Attention Was Never Compute-Bound
posts.subtitle: The bottleneck was never FLOPs — it was reading and writing GPU memory
posts.summary: Standard attention materializes a full N×N score matrix in slow GPU memory (HBM), making it memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. FlashAttention fuses the whole computation into tiled blocks kept in fast on-chip SRAM using an online softmax trick, computing mathematically exact attention while cutting HBM traffic and turning quadratic memory into linear.

slides.title: GPUs Are Compute-Rich But Memory-Bandwidth-Poor
slides.body: A modern GPU can do far more math per second than it can move bytes between its slow high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and its fast on-chip SRAM. Standard attention ignores this and pays for it — FlashAttention was built specifically to stop paying it.

slides.title: Standard Attention Materializes an N×N Matrix in Slow Memory
bullets: Computing attention naively builds the full query-key score matrix (N tokens × N tokens) and writes it out to HBM before softmax, then reads it back for the weighted sum with values
That matrix grows quadratically with sequence length — double the context, quadruple the memory traffic

GPU on-chip SRAM is tiny compared to HBM but roughly an order of magnitude faster to read/write — naive attention barely uses it, spending most of its time waiting on HBM round-trips rather than doing math
This makes standard attention memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound — the GPU's math units sit idle waiting for data

slides.title: Tile the Computation, Never Materialize the Full Matrix
bullets: FlashAttention splits queries, keys, and values into small blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM
It computes attention block-by-block, fusing the score, softmax, and weighted-sum steps into one kernel so intermediate results never get written back out to HBM
An online softmax trick keeps a running max and running sum as blocks are processed, so the full row of scores never needs to exist in memory at once — the math still comes out exact
Because it's a kernel-fusion and I/O-scheduling technique, not an approximation, FlashAttention returns bit-for-bit the same result as standard attention — just computed with far less memory traffic

slides.title: The Real Bottleneck Was I/O, Not FLOPs
bullets: The paper's core insight: at the sequence lengths modern transformers use, attention's runtime is dominated by memory accesses, not arithmetic — an I/O complexity analysis, not just a speed hack
Standard attention does roughly O(N²) reads and writes to slow HBM; FlashAttention's tiling reduces that traffic by keeping working blocks resident in SRAM as long as possible
Total FLOPs computed doesn't go down — FlashAttention doesn't reduce the math, it stops paying for unnecessary trips to slow memory to do that same math

slides.title: Worked Example: Training on 16K-Token Sequences
slides.body: Training a model with 16K-token context, standard attention per layer per head needs a 16K × 16K score matrix — over 256 million entries — written to and read from HBM.
bullets: That matrix alone can exceed available memory well before the model weights do, forcing shorter sequences or smaller batches just to fit
FlashAttention never forms that full matrix — it processes tiles small enough for SRAM, so peak memory for attention grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically
This is what let longer-context training and inference become practical without needing proportionally more GPU memory just for attention itself

slides.title: Standard Attention vs. FlashAttention

rows: Exact — bit-identical math, not an approximation
Compute (SRAM keeps data close to the math units)
Full score matrix ever materialized in HBM?

slides.title: Where It Doesn't Help
bullets: It doesn't reduce total FLOPs — attention is still O(N²) compute, so extremely long sequences eventually hit a compute wall FlashAttention alone can't remove
The speedup comes from hand-tuned CUDA kernels matched to specific GPU generations — a naive PyTorch reimplementation of the algorithm on paper won't get the same win without that kernel engineering

It has to be wired into the model's attention layer explicitly; frameworks and hardware need to support the fused kernel (FlashAttention-2 and -3 exist specifically because each new GPU generation needed re-tuned kernels)

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Attention's real bottleneck at typical sequence lengths is GPU memory bandwidth, not raw compute
FlashAttention fuses score, softmax, and weighted-sum into tiled kernels that never materialize the full N×N matrix in slow HBM, using an online softmax to stay exact
Memory scales linearly instead of quadratically with sequence length — a structural enabler for longer context, not just a constant-factor speedup
It's exact, not approximate — the output matches standard attention bit-for-bit, so there's no accuracy tradeoff to weigh against the speed

questions.prompt: What is FlashAttention's core technique?
options: Approximating attention with a sparse pattern

Distilling attention into a smaller learned function

questions.explanation: FlashAttention processes attention in small tiles kept in fast on-chip SRAM, using an online softmax so the full score matrix never needs to be materialized in slow HBM.

questions.prompt: Is FlashAttention's output an approximation of standard attention?
options: Yes, it trades a small accuracy loss for speed
No — it computes mathematically exact attention, just with far less memory traffic
Yes, but only for sequences longer than 8K tokens
It depends on the GPU generation
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is a kernel-fusion and I/O-scheduling technique, not an approximation — the online softmax trick lets it produce the exact same result as standard attention.

questions.prompt: What bottleneck does FlashAttention primarily target?
options: Network bandwidth between GPUs in a cluster
Disk I/O when loading model checkpoints
GPU memory bandwidth — the cost of moving data between HBM and on-chip SRAM
CPU-side tokenization speed
questions.explanation: At the sequence lengths transformers use, standard attention is bound by how much data it moves in and out of slow HBM, not by how much arithmetic the GPU can do — that's the bottleneck FlashAttention removes.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Search Avoids Comparing Everything
posts.subtitle: A layered graph that turns a billion-vector search into a few dozen hops.
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph structure behind most production vector databases' default index. It trades a small, tunable amount of recall for roughly logarithmic query time by searching a layered proximity graph instead of scanning every vector.

slides.title: Vector Search Doesn't Scan Every Vector
slides.body: At a billion embeddings, comparing a query to every vector turns milliseconds into seconds. HNSW is the graph structure behind almost every production vector database's default index.

slides.title: Brute-Force kNN Doesn't Scale
bullets: Exact k-nearest-neighbors is O(N) per query — with 100M 768-dim vectors, that's billions of float comparisons per search.
RAG retrieval latency budgets are usually under 50ms; brute force blows past that once N reaches a few million.
Sharding buys parallelism but doesn't fix the underlying linear scan per shard.

slides.title: A Graph Where Nearby Points Are Neighbors
bullets: HNSW builds a proximity graph: each vector is a node linked to its approximate nearest neighbors.
The graph is layered like a skip list — top layers are sparse 'highways' with few nodes, the bottom layer holds every point.
Search starts at the top layer's single entry point and greedily walks toward the query, dropping a layer each time no neighbor gets closer.

slides.title: Two Knobs Control the Speed/Recall Tradeoff
bullets: M: max neighbors per node (commonly 16-64). Higher M means better recall but more memory.
efConstruction: candidate list size while building the graph — higher gives a better-connected graph but slower indexing.
efSearch: candidate list size at query time — the one knob you can tune live to trade latency for recall, no rebuild needed.

slides.title: HNSW vs. the Alternatives
Example: Finding Similar Docs Among 50M Embeddings
bullets: Query embedding enters at the top layer's single entry point.
At each layer, search greedily moves to whichever neighbor is closest to the query, stopping when nothing improves — then drops a layer.
By the bottom layer, the search is already near the true neighborhood; a wider local search (sized by efSearch) finds the final top-k.
Total comparisons: often just tens to hundreds, not 50 million.

slides.title: When HNSW Is the Wrong Choice
bullets: Memory-hungry: graph edges plus vectors often need 1.5-2x the raw vector data in RAM — expensive at billion-scale.
Deletes are awkward — HNSW graphs are built incrementally, so cleanly removing a node usually means tombstoning or a partial rebuild.
For small collections (roughly under 10K vectors), brute force is often just as fast with none of the graph-traversal overhead.
Filtered search ('nearest neighbors where category=X') can break the graph's locality assumptions and hurt recall.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: HNSW trades a small, tunable accuracy loss for roughly logarithmic query time — the default index in Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and pgvector's HNSW mode.
Tune efSearch first — it's the one knob you can change per-query without rebuilding the index.
At small scale, or when you need guaranteed exact recall, skip the graph and brute-force it instead.

questions.prompt: Why does HNSW avoid comparing a query to every vector in the collection?
options: It only checks the first N vectors alphabetically
It walks a layered proximity graph, greedily hopping toward the query
It stores vectors in a hash table that needs no comparisons
It reduces every vector to a single bit before comparing
questions.explanation: HNSW's search greedily traverses graph edges toward the query, stopping when no neighbor is closer — that yields roughly logarithmic, not linear, query cost.

questions.prompt: Which parameter can you increase at query time, without rebuilding the index, to trade latency for higher recall?
options: M
efConstruction
efSearch
nlist
questions.explanation: efSearch controls how many candidates the search keeps and is read at query time, so it can be tuned per-query. M and efConstruction are baked in when the graph is built.

questions.prompt: When is brute-force nearest-neighbor search often the better choice over HNSW?
options: Never — HNSW always wins
On very small collections, or when exact recall is required
When vectors are high-dimensional
When queries arrive one at a time
questions.explanation: At small N, graph-traversal overhead doesn't pay for itself, and HNSW is inherently approximate — if guaranteed exact results are required, brute force (or an exact index) is the only correct option.

posts.title: Agent Memory: State That Outlives One Context Window
posts.subtitle: Why long-running agents need more than just a bigger context window.
posts.summary: LLM calls are stateless — nothing persists across sessions unless you explicitly store and re-inject it. Agent memory is the engineering layer that decides what a long-running agent keeps: working context for the current task, episodic logs of past interactions, and a curated store of durable facts.

slides.title: An Agent That Forgets Everything Every Session
slides.body: Every LLM call is stateless — the model has no memory unless you put it back in the prompt. 'Agent memory' is the engineering layer that decides what comes back.

slides.title: The Context Window Is Not Memory
bullets: A large context window still resets to zero on the next session — nothing persists unless it's explicitly stored and re-injected.
Replaying the entire history every call burns tokens linearly with conversation length and degrades attention over long inputs.
Long-running agents (coding agents, support bots) need facts from days or weeks ago — far outside any single context window.

slides.title: Three Layers: Working, Episodic, Semantic
bullets: Working memory: the live context window — the current task's scratchpad, cleared or summarized each session.
Episodic memory: a log of past interactions, retrieved by recency or similarity — a vector store of past turns and summaries.
Semantic memory: durable facts extracted and deduplicated over time (preferences, conventions) — small, curated, always injected.

slides.title: How It Actually Gets Built
bullets: Summarization: periodically compress old turns into a running summary instead of keeping the raw transcript.
Retrieval: embed past turns/notes and pull back only the top-k relevant ones — the same mechanism as RAG, aimed at the agent's own history.
Write-time extraction: after a session, a separate call extracts durable facts ('deploy target is us-east-1') into a structured store.

slides.title: Four Memory Strategies, Four Failure Modes

rows: Hits context limit, buries signal in noise
Lossy — can silently drop a detail that mattered later
Cheap per call, needs an embedding store
Misses relevant memories that aren't semantically similar
Needs reliable extraction; facts go stale if never updated

slides.title: Example: A Coding Agent Across Three Sessions
bullets: Session 1: user says 'we use pnpm, not npm' — extracted into the fact store.
Session 2 (next day, fresh context): the agent injects the fact store first, sees 'pnpm', and runs the right install command unprompted.
Session 3: user asks about a bug discussed two weeks ago — too specific for the fact store, so the agent runs a retrieval query over episodic logs instead of replaying the whole history.

slides.title: Where Agent Memory Goes Wrong
bullets: Unbounded fact stores become their own retrieval problem — hundreds of stored 'facts' need the same relevance filtering raw documents do.
Silent staleness: a fact extracted once ('user works at Acme') never gets invalidated when it's no longer true.
Over-summarization loses the specific detail an edge case needed — summaries optimize for the common case, not the exception.
Retrieval-based memory can miss things that matter but aren't textually or semantically similar to the current query.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Memory is an engineering choice, not a model feature — you decide what's summarized, retrieved, or discarded.
Match the layer to the data: durable preferences go in structured facts, conversation history goes through retrieval, the current task stays in working context.
Budget for staleness and forgetting on purpose — memory that never expires becomes noise, not signal.

questions.prompt: Why can't a large context window alone serve as an agent's long-term memory?
options: Context windows can't hold text, only numbers

questions.explanation: Statelessness is the core issue: however large the window, it's gone once the call ends. Persistence requires an external store plus a retrieval/injection step.

questions.prompt: A user's fixed preference like 'always use pnpm' is best stored as which kind of memory?
options: Working memory only
Episodic memory (raw transcript log)
A structured/semantic fact store
It should never be persisted
questions.explanation: Durable, stable facts belong in a curated structured store that's cheaply injected every session — retrieval or full-transcript approaches serve less predictable, history-shaped queries, not fixed facts.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of rolling summarization as a memory strategy?
options: It's too expensive to run

It only works for coding agents

questions.explanation: Summarization compresses for the common case; an edge-case detail that seemed unimportant when summarized can vanish from the record entirely, with no signal that it was dropped.

posts.title: Requests and Limits: Why Kubernetes Kills Some Pods
posts.subtitle: Requests decide where a pod is scheduled. Limits decide what happens when it goes over.
posts.summary: Kubernetes uses two separate numbers per container — requests and limits — for CPU and memory, and they're enforced completely differently. Requests are what the scheduler bin-packs nodes against; limits are a hard ceiling enforced by the kernel's cgroups. Go over a memory limit and the kernel OOM-kills the container instantly; go over a CPU limit and the container is merely throttled, never killed. Understanding that asymmetry explains most 'why did my pod just restart' incidents.

slides.title: Two numbers per container, enforced two completely different ways
slides.body: Every Kubernetes container can declare a CPU/memory request and a CPU/memory limit. They look symmetric in the YAML, but the scheduler and the kernel treat them very differently — and that difference is why some pods get OOMKilled while others just quietly slow down.

slides.title: Requests answer 'where', limits answer 'what if it goes over'
bullets: requests.cpu / requests.memory: what the scheduler reserves on a node when deciding to place the pod — the scheduler only ever bin-packs against requests, never limits
limits.cpu / limits.memory: the hard ceiling the container is allowed to use once it's running, enforced by the node's kernel via cgroups
If you set no requests at all, the scheduler treats the pod as needing (effectively) nothing — it can land on an already-busy node and starve
If you set limits far above requests, a node can end up overcommitted: the sum of running pods' actual usage can exceed what the node physically has, even though every pod is within its own limit

slides.title: Memory is killed, CPU is throttled
slides.body: The two resource types hit fundamentally different cgroup mechanisms when a container exceeds its limit.
bullets: Memory is incompressible: a process can't be 'slowed down' to use less RAM, so exceeding memory.max in the container's cgroup makes the kernel OOM-kill the process immediately (exit code 137, reason OOMKilled)

CPU is compressible: exceeding the CPU limit doesn't kill anything — the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller just throttles the container, denying it CPU time for the rest of each scheduling period until usage drops back under quota

That's why a memory leak crashes a pod in a visible restart loop, while a CPU-hungry pod just gets slower and slower with no crash at all — worth checking `kubectl top pod` and throttling metrics before assuming a slow pod is a code bug
A killed container is restarted according to the pod's restartPolicy, which is why OOMKilled pods commonly show up as CrashLoopBackOff after repeated kills

slides.title: Requests vs limits set a pod's QoS class
slides.body: Kubernetes derives a Quality-of-Service class from how requests and limits compare, and that class decides eviction order under node pressure.
bullets: Guaranteed: every container sets requests == limits for both CPU and memory — the pod gets the strongest eviction protection
Burstable: at least one container sets a request, and at least one request/limit pair differs — normal middle-ground behavior for most workloads
BestEffort: no requests or limits set on any container at all — first in line to be evicted the moment a node runs low on resources
Under memory pressure, the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods using more memory than they requested, and only reaches Guaranteed pods as a last resort

slides.title: Worked example: a pod set with request=256Mi, limit=512Mi
slides.body: A container declares requests.memory: 256Mi and limits.memory: 512Mi.
bullets: Scheduling: the scheduler only counts the 256Mi request against the node's allocatable memory when deciding whether the pod fits
Normal operation: the container can grow past 256Mi (that number is not enforced as a ceiling) and run anywhere up to 512Mi without issue
A traffic spike pushes usage to 600Mi: the cgroup memory.max is 512Mi, so the kernel OOM-kills the container the instant it crosses that line — not gradually, immediately
If the equivalent CPU had been requests: 250m, limits: 500m instead, the same overshoot would just throttle the container's CPU time — no kill, no restart, just added latency

slides.title: Same shape, opposite consequences

rows: Throttled — denied CPU time for the rest of the period

slides.title: Common pitfalls
bullets: Omitting requests entirely lets the scheduler pack a node far past its real capacity, since it thinks the pod needs nothing — every pod in a namespace should have requests, enforced with a LimitRange if needed
Setting memory limit == real steady-state usage with no headroom guarantees an OOM-kill on the first minor spike (a GC pause, a burst of concurrent requests) — leave real margin
Setting CPU limits too tight silently degrades latency-sensitive services through throttling that doesn't show up as an error anywhere except CPU-throttling metrics
Copy-pasting requests/limits across services with very different workload shapes (bursty vs steady) bakes in either wasted reserved capacity or surprise evictions

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Requests drive scheduling (bin-packing against a node's allocatable capacity); limits drive runtime enforcement via cgroups
Memory limits kill on overshoot because memory is incompressible; CPU limits only throttle because CPU time is compressible
requests vs limits also sets the pod's QoS class (Guaranteed/Burstable/BestEffort), which decides eviction order under node pressure
Always set requests close to real steady-state usage and leave real headroom on memory limits — that single habit prevents most OOMKill incidents

questions.prompt: What does the Kubernetes scheduler use to decide which node a pod fits on?
options: The pod's limits
The pod's requests

questions.explanation: The scheduler bin-packs against requests, not limits. A pod with no requests set is treated as needing effectively nothing, which is how nodes end up overcommitted.

questions.prompt: A container exceeds its memory limit. What happens?
options: The kernel throttles it, denying memory allocations until usage drops
Nothing — memory limits are only advisory
The kernel OOM-kills the container immediately because memory can't be throttled
Kubernetes automatically raises the limit
questions.explanation: Memory is incompressible — a process can't be slowed down to use less of it — so cgroups enforce the memory limit by killing the container the instant it crosses memory.max.

questions.prompt: Under node memory pressure, which pods does the kubelet evict first?
options: Guaranteed pods (requests == limits)
BestEffort pods (no requests or limits set)
Whichever pod has been running the longest
Pods are evicted in random order regardless of QoS class
questions.explanation: BestEffort pods have no resource guarantees at all, so they're evicted first. Burstable pods using more than they requested go next, and Guaranteed pods are protected until last.

posts.title: Tree of Thoughts: Letting an LLM Backtrack
posts.subtitle: Chain-of-thought commits to one path. Tree of Thoughts explores several and prunes the bad ones.
posts.summary: Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) turns LLM reasoning from a single linear chain into an explicit search tree: the model generates several candidate next steps, a self-evaluation step scores each one, and a search algorithm (BFS or DFS) decides which branches to keep exploring and which to abandon. It costs many more model calls than plain chain-of-thought, but on tasks that need planning and backtracking, that extra compute buys a large jump in success rate.

slides.title: One wrong step early in a chain dooms the whole answer
slides.body: Chain-of-thought prompting makes an LLM show its reasoning, but it still only ever commits to one path. Tree of Thoughts (ToT) instead treats reasoning as a search problem: generate multiple next steps, evaluate them, and backtrack when a branch looks bad.

slides.title: Chain-of-thought can't undo a bad move
bullets: Standard CoT samples one linear sequence of reasoning steps token by token, left to right, with no mechanism to revisit an earlier step
On tasks that need planning or search (puzzles, multi-step math, creative writing with constraints), a single greedy path frequently locks in a mistake it can't recover from
Self-consistency (sampling many full CoT chains and majority-voting the final answer) helps but still evaluates each chain only at the very end — it can't prune a bad path early to save compute
The model has no way to look ahead, compare partial solutions against each other, or explicitly decide 'this direction isn't working, try another'

slides.title: Four pieces turn reasoning into a search problem
slides.body: ToT frames problem solving as maintaining a tree of 'thoughts' — coherent, self-contained intermediate steps — and defines four things the problem author must specify.
bullets: Thought decomposition: break the solution into steps small enough to evaluate independently, but large enough to carry real information (e.g. one equation, one paragraph, one partial plan)
Thought generator: propose the next thoughts from a given state, either by sampling several independent completions or by asking for a batch of distinct proposals in one prompt
State evaluator: have the LLM itself judge each partial state — either assign a scalar value ('sure/likely/impossible') or vote between candidates — to estimate how promising it is

Search algorithm: use the evaluator's scores to decide which thoughts survive; ToT typically uses breadth-first search (keep the top-b states per level) or depth-first search (commit to one path, backtrack on failure or a low score)

slides.title: BFS-ToT: expand, score, keep the top b, repeat
slides.body: The most common setup is breadth-first: at every level of the tree, generate several candidate next-thoughts per surviving state, score all of them, and keep only the top b before expanding the next level.
bullets: b (the 'beam width') controls the quality/cost tradeoff directly — b=1 degrades toward greedy CoT, larger b explores more branches at proportionally higher token cost
Pruning happens level by level, so a branch that scores as 'impossible' gets dropped before the model wastes calls extending it further
Because generation and evaluation are separate LLM calls, the same base model plays both roles — no separate reward model or fine-tuning is required
DFS-ToT is a cheaper variant: follow the most promising thought until a score drops below a threshold or a max depth is hit, then backtrack to the parent and try the next candidate

slides.title: Worked example: Game of 24
slides.body: Task: combine four numbers (e.g. 4, 9, 10, 13) with +, -, x, / to reach exactly 24, using each number once.
bullets: Thought decomposition: each 'thought' is one arithmetic step that combines two of the remaining numbers into a new number
Thought generator: from {4, 9, 10, 13}, propose several first moves — e.g. 13-9=4, 10-4=6, 4x9=36 — each leaving a shorter list to keep solving

State evaluator: the LLM checks each resulting set for whether 24 still looks reachable ('sure' / 'maybe' / 'impossible'), pruning states like the one left with only very large or very small remaining numbers

Search keeps the top b=5 states per step and expands each; the surviving branch that reaches [24] with an unused-number count of zero is the answer: 13-9=4, 4x6=24 combined with 10-4=6 gives (13-9)x(10-4)=24

slides.title: More search, more cost, more reliability

rows: Many independent chains, vote at the end
Explicit tree, evaluated and pruned per step
Can abandon a bad step mid-way?
No — only discovered at the final vote
Yes — low-scoring states are pruned immediately
Roughly N x depth (generation + evaluation at every level)
Yes — BFS or DFS over states
Tasks where multiple independent tries help
Planning, puzzles, tasks with a checkable intermediate state

slides.title: When Tree of Thoughts is the wrong tool
bullets: Token cost scales with beam width and depth — for straightforward tasks that a single CoT pass already solves reliably, ToT just burns extra calls for no gain

It depends on the model being a decent judge of its own partial progress; if the state evaluator can't reliably tell 'promising' from 'dead end', the search prunes good branches or wastes budget on bad ones
The thought decomposition has to be designed per task — there's no universal 'right' granularity, and a bad decomposition (steps too coarse or too fine) weakens the whole search
Latency is much higher than single-pass CoT, since branches are typically evaluated in sequence or in small batches rather than one shot

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: ToT = thought decomposition + generator + evaluator + search — it turns reasoning into an explicit, prunable search tree instead of one committed chain
The model plays two roles itself: proposing next steps and judging how promising each one is — no separate trained reward model needed
It buys reliability on tasks with a checkable intermediate state and real planning demands, at a real multiple in token cost and latency over plain CoT
Reach for it when a task needs backtracking or lookahead; skip it when a single reasoning pass already gets the answer right most of the time

questions.prompt: What can Tree of Thoughts do that a single chain-of-thought pass cannot?
options: Run without any LLM calls
Abandon a low-scoring partial solution mid-way and try a different branch
Guarantee a correct answer on every task
Skip the need for a thought decomposition
questions.explanation: Plain CoT commits to one linear path token by token. ToT scores partial states as it goes and can prune or backtrack away from a branch that looks unpromising, instead of only finding out at the very end.

questions.prompt: In BFS-style Tree of Thoughts, what does the beam width b control?
options: The number of tokens in each thought
How many top-scoring states are kept and expanded at each level of the tree
The temperature used for sampling
Whether the search uses depth-first or breadth-first traversal
questions.explanation: At each level, every surviving state proposes several next thoughts; the evaluator scores them and only the top b are kept for the next round. Small b approaches greedy CoT, larger b explores more but costs more.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a real limitation of Tree of Thoughts?
options: It cannot be implemented with the same base model that does the reasoning
It requires a separately trained reward model
Its cost scales with beam width and depth, and it depends on the model being a reliable judge of its own partial progress
It only works on natural-language tasks, never on math or puzzles
questions.explanation: ToT reuses the same LLM for both generating and evaluating thoughts, so no separate reward model is needed. Its real costs are the multiplied token/latency budget and its reliance on the model's self-evaluation being trustworthy.

posts.title: SimWAM: Train With Video, Deploy Without It
posts.subtitle: A driving planner that borrows video generation's instincts, then throws the video model away
posts.summary: SimWAM co-trains a video-generation expert and a lightweight action expert with shared flow matching, then discards the video branch at deployment — keeping only a fast, self-contained trajectory planner. It hits 91.5 PDMS on NAVSIM's navtest split, beating both a VLM-based planner and prior world-action models that still generate video at inference, while running with lower latency.

slides.title: One camera, no future-frame gambling
slides.body: SimWAM is a world-action model for autonomous driving that borrows motion knowledge from video generation during training, then throws the video branch away at deployment, leaving a fast, self-contained planner.

slides.title: World-action models pay a latency tax to "imagine" the future
slides.body: Prior world-action models like DriveWAM and DriveLaW generate candidate future video frames at inference time to reason about what might happen next, then pick a trajectory — that generation step is slow.
bullets: Generating even short video rollouts at inference adds real latency, a hard problem for a planner that must act roughly every 100ms
Yet dropping the video signal entirely throws away motion priors learned from large-scale driving video
The field was stuck choosing between "slow but well-informed" and "fast but shallow"

slides.title: Co-train two experts, deploy only one
slides.body: SimWAM jointly trains a pretrained video expert and a lightweight action expert with shared flow matching, connected only through attention — then discards the video branch after training.
bullets: An "isolated attention mask" keeps action-token predictions independent of future video frames — the only structural change needed to let the branches separate cleanly
The two experts share no parameters, so the video backbone can be swapped or the action expert scaled independently without touching the training objective
A reinforcement learning pass (FlowGRPO) further optimizes trajectory predictions against driving rewards, beyond plain imitation of the training data

slides.title: Higher accuracy than the models it trades speed against
slides.body: On NAVSIM's navtest benchmark, SimWAM edges out both a VLM-based planner and prior WAM-based planners on PDMS, while running with the lowest latency of the world-model-based group — since it never generates video at inference.

slides.title: Worked case: single front camera, zero future frames
slides.body: At inference, SimWAM takes one 384x672 front-camera frame, runs it through the surviving action expert only, and outputs a trajectory directly — no rollout, no sampled future video.
bullets: The trained model transfers zero-shot to nuScenes, a different driving dataset than NAVSIM, without retraining — a sign the motion priors learned during co-training generalize past one benchmark
The video expert that shaped those priors during training never runs at deployment time, so inference-time cost stays close to a plain action-only planner
That's the practical payoff of the isolated attention mask: the GPU budget that would go to generating video instead goes to trajectory accuracy

slides.title: Where this trades away, and what it assumes
slides.body: SimWAM's inference-time speed comes from a specific training-time choice, not a free lunch.
bullets: The video expert still has to be trained (a pretrained one, Wan2.2, is used as the starting point) — the co-training cost is real even though inference doesn't pay it
Reported results use a single front-camera setup at 384x672 — multi-camera or higher-resolution deployments aren't part of the released benchmarks
Zero-shot transfer to nuScenes is promising but is one dataset, not proof the priors generalize to arbitrary driving conditions or geographies
If inference-time speed isn't the constraint (e.g., offline simulation), a model that keeps the video rollout may still give more interpretable failure cases

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Video generation is used as a training-time teacher, not a deployment-time requirement — the branch that shaped the model's motion priors can be discarded once it has done its job
An isolated attention mask is the whole mechanism enabling the split: it just has to stop action tokens from depending on future frames
91.5 PDMS on NAVSIM navtest beats a VLM-based planner (91.1) and prior WAM-based planners that keep video generation at inference (90.1, 89.1) — with lower latency
Zero-shot transfer to nuScenes suggests the approach isn't overfit to one benchmark, but multi-camera and higher-resolution setups remain unproven

questions.explanation: SimWAM trains a video expert and action expert jointly, but the isolated attention mask means the action expert never depended on the video branch's outputs — so at inference it can run alone, skipping the costly video generation step prior WAMs rely on.

questions.prompt: What mechanism allows the video and action experts to be separated after training?
options: A shared parameter matrix that averages both experts
An isolated attention mask that keeps action-token predictions independent of future video frames

questions.explanation: The isolated attention mask is the single structural change: it prevents action predictions from attending to future frames, so the two experts only interact through attention during training and can be cleanly split afterward.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Tokens to Skip Ahead
posts.subtitle: A small draft model proposes tokens; the big model verifies them all in one pass
posts.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by having a small draft model propose several tokens ahead, then verifying all of them in a single forward pass of the large target model. A rejection-sampling rule guarantees the output is statistically identical to plain decoding — so the speedup (commonly 2-3x) comes at no quality cost, as long as the draft model's guesses are accurate enough to be worth checking.

slides.title: Why decode one token at a time when a cheap model can guess several?
slides.body: Autoregressive LLM decoding generates one token per forward pass, and each pass reads the model's full weights from memory. Speculative decoding lets a small, fast model draft ahead so the big model can verify multiple tokens per pass instead of generating them one by one.

slides.title: Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound
slides.body: Generating each token requires streaming the full set of model weights from memory, even though a single token only needs a tiny amount of arithmetic. At batch size 1, the GPU spends most of its time waiting on memory bandwidth, not doing math.
bullets: A 70B model in fp16 needs roughly 140GB of weights read from memory for every single token generated
The actual compute for one token (a handful of matrix multiplies) is tiny next to the memory traffic required to read those weights
Larger batches amortize this cost across more tokens, but a single interactive user pays the full memory-bandwidth cost per token

slides.title: Draft small, verify big, accept what matches
slides.body: Speculative decoding runs a small draft model to propose K tokens ahead cheaply, then does one forward pass of the large target model to score all K draft tokens plus the next one at once — accepting drafted tokens that match what the big model would have generated anyway.
bullets: The draft model (often 10-100x smaller) proposes tokens autoregressively, which is cheap because it's small
The target model scores the entire drafted sequence in a single forward pass — the same memory-bandwidth cost as generating one token, but now covering K+1 candidate positions

A rejection-sampling rule accepts each drafted token with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft), guaranteeing the final output distribution is mathematically identical to plain decoding from the target model alone

slides.title: Why acceptance rate decides everything
slides.body: The speedup from speculative decoding depends entirely on how often the draft model's guesses match what the target model would have said.
bullets: If the draft and target models agree often (predictable text), acceptance rate can reach 70-90%, giving close to K-times fewer expensive target passes
If they disagree often (creative or technical text where the draft model predicts poorly), acceptance drops and speedup shrinks toward 1x
The moment a draft token is rejected, decoding falls back to sampling that one position from the target model directly, then speculation restarts from there
Picking K (how many tokens to draft ahead) is a trade-off: too small wastes the opportunity, too large means paying for draft tokens that get rejected anyway

slides.title: Same output distribution, fewer expensive passes
slides.body: The property that makes this safe for production: verified speculative decoding produces exactly the same output distribution as running the target model alone — it's a speedup, not an approximation.

rows: N (one per token, on small model)

slides.title: Worked example: drafting 4 tokens for "The capital of France is"
slides.body: Suppose the draft model proposes ["Paris", ",", " a", " city"] after "The capital of France is". The target model scores all 4 positions plus one more in a single pass.
bullets: "Paris" matches what the target model would have picked (high probability) → accepted
"," matches → accepted
" a" — the target model actually preferred " known" here → rejected; decoding samples " known" from the target model's distribution at this position
Everything drafted after the rejection point (" city") is discarded, and the next round of drafting restarts from " known"
Net result: 2 tokens accepted for free, 1 corrected, for roughly the cost of one target-model forward pass instead of three

slides.title: When speculative decoding doesn't help
slides.body: It's a wall-clock latency optimization, not a free win in every setting.
bullets: At large batch sizes, decoding is already compute-bound rather than memory-bound, so there's less idle bandwidth for the draft model to exploit — gains shrink
You need a draft model that's both cheap and well-aligned with the target model's outputs; a poorly matched draft model (different tokenizer, very different training data) tails off toward 1x speedup
Serving two models (draft + target) adds memory footprint and engineering complexity versus serving one
On highly unpredictable text, low acceptance rates can occasionally make it slightly slower than plain decoding because of draft-model overhead

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth bound at small batch sizes — the bottleneck is reading weights, not doing math — which is exactly the idle capacity this trick exploits
A small draft model proposes tokens; one target-model forward pass verifies all of them via rejection sampling
The output distribution is mathematically identical to plain decoding — this is a latency optimization with no quality cost, not an approximation
Real-world speedups (commonly 2-3x) depend entirely on acceptance rate, which depends on how well the draft model matches the target model's behavior

questions.prompt: Why is single-token LLM decoding usually memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound?
options: GPUs cannot do floating point math fast enough
Generating one token requires streaming the full set of model weights from memory, while the actual arithmetic for one token is comparatively tiny
The tokenizer is the slowest part of the pipeline
Network latency dominates every forward pass
questions.explanation: At batch size 1, each decoding step has to read the entire model's weights from GPU memory to compute a single token, so the GPU spends most of its time waiting on memory bandwidth rather than doing math — this is exactly the idle capacity speculative decoding exploits.

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding doesn't change the quality of the generated text?
options: The draft model is trained to be identical to the target model
A rejection-sampling acceptance rule ensures the final output distribution exactly matches sampling from the target model alone
Only the first drafted token is ever used
The target model re-generates the entire sequence from scratch afterward
questions.explanation: Each drafted token is accepted with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft) and rejected tokens are resampled from a corrected distribution — this rejection-sampling scheme is mathematically proven to reproduce the target model's exact output distribution.

questions.prompt: What most directly determines the speedup you get from speculative decoding?
options: The size of the target model alone
The acceptance rate — how often the draft model's guesses match what the target model would have produced
The number of GPUs used
The length of the prompt
questions.explanation: High acceptance rate means most drafted tokens get confirmed in a single cheap verification pass, multiplying effective throughput; low acceptance rate means frequent fallback to single-token generation, and speedup collapses toward 1x.
